title: Present-Day Safety Evidence Log
summary: Logs evidence from daily life that the client's current environment is safe, to counter a persistent sense of danger.
goal: Help the client's nervous system gather evidence that today is not the same as the past.
body_md: Each day, have the client note one piece of concrete evidence that their current environment and relationships are safe, a locked door, a trusted person nearby, a boundary that was respected. This builds a body of present-day evidence over time without ever asking the client to revisit or describe what happened previously. Review the accumulating log together in session.

fields.label: Today's evidence of safety
How much my body believed it, out of ten
What helped it land, if anything
What I want to notice more of this week

title: Self-Compassion for the Younger Self Practice
summary: Practices directing compassion toward a younger version of the client who went through a hard experience.
goal: Offer the client's present self a way to extend compassion to a younger self, without revisiting details.
body_md: Ask the client to picture a younger version of themselves and write what they would want that younger self to know now, without describing what happened to them. Keep the focus entirely on comfort and compassion directed at the younger self, not on narrating events. Some clients find this easier through drawing or a photo rather than direct visualization; either is fine.

fields.label: What I would want my younger self to know
How I would want to comfort them
What I notice in my body doing this practice
What my present self needs to hear too

title: Grounding Through the Body Practice
summary: A body-based grounding sequence for use when a client feels pulled out of the present moment.
goal: Give the client a reliable, body-based way back to the present when it starts to slip.
body_md: Walk through pressing feet into the floor, naming the temperature of the air, and noticing a point of contact with a chair or the ground, slowly and in session first. This is a stabilizing skill and is not paired with any request to recall or narrate past events. If the practice ever brings up thoughts of self-harm, pause and address it directly in session, with 988 (call or text) available right away.

fields.label: What I feel pressing into the floor
The temperature of the air around me
A point of contact I can notice
How grounded I feel now compared to before (0 to 10)
If thoughts of self-harm come up, what I will do (988, call or text)

title: Supporting a Partner Who Is a Survivor Sheet
summary: Helps the non-survivor partner learn what supportive, non-pressuring responses look like day to day.
goal: Give a supporting partner concrete, low-pressure ways to be helpful without pushing for more than the survivor is ready for.
body_md: The supporting partner often wants to help but is unsure what is welcome, so this has the survivor name what support currently feels good, patience with physical closeness, not asking questions, checking in without pressure, while the supporting partner names their own questions or worries separately. Keep the focus on present-day support needs, not on discussing what happened. Revisit as needs shift over time.

fields.label: Survivor: what support feels good right now
Survivor: what does not feel good right now
Supporting partner: a worry I have about getting this right
Supporting partner: what I will try instead
How this conversation felt for each of us

title: Coping Toolbox Craft
summary: A child decorates a small box and fills it with reminders of coping skills that actually work for them.
goal: Give a child a physical, personalized collection of their own working coping skills.
body_md: The parent and child decorate a small box together, then fill it with cards or small objects representing coping skills that have actually worked before, a stress ball, a breathing card, a photo of a calming place. The child picks what goes in based on their own experience, not a generic list. Keep the box somewhere easy to reach during a hard moment.

fields.label: A coping skill I put in my box
Why I picked it
Another skill I added
A time this week I used something from my box

title: Coping Skill Speed Match Game
summary: Players race to match a distressing scenario card with the coping skill card that fits it best.
goal: Build quick recall of which coping skill fits which kind of distress.
body_md: Lay out scenario cards and coping skill cards, then have players race, individually or in teams, to make the fastest correct matches, discussing any disputed pairing afterward since more than one skill can often fit. This builds quick recall under a bit of pressure, closer to how skill use actually needs to work in real moments. Close by asking each player their go-to match.

fields.label: A match I made quickly
A match that was disputed
My personal go-to skill for a tough scenario
A skill I want to get better at reaching for

title: Coping Skill Context Map
summary: Sorts a client's coping skills by the setting they are actually usable in, home, work, in public.
goal: Match coping skills to where the client can realistically use them, not just what sounds good on paper.
body_md: A coping skill that works well at home may be impossible to use discreetly at work, so this sorts the client's known skills by setting: private and unlimited, at work, in public, in front of others. Identify any setting with no usable skill yet and brainstorm one that would actually fit there. This turns a general coping list into something usable in the moment it is actually needed.

fields.label: Skills that work at home
Skills that work at work or school
Skills that work in public
A setting with no skill yet
A skill to try building for that setting

title: Coping Skill Cost and Payoff Sheet
summary: Weighs the short-term relief and longer-term cost of a client's current coping habits.
goal: Help the client see which coping habits are worth keeping and which are worth replacing.
body_md: List the client's current go-to coping habits, healthy and less healthy alike, and rate each for short-term relief and longer-term cost side by side. Some habits will score well on both, some will trade a small relief for a larger cost, and naming that plainly makes the tradeoff visible without moralizing about it. Pick one habit to work on shifting first.

fields.label: A current coping habit
Short-term relief it provides
Longer-term cost, if any
Another habit and the same rating
Which habit I want to shift first

title: Values-Matched Coping Menu
summary: Builds a coping skills menu filtered through which ones actually fit the client's values, not just what is calming.
goal: Choose coping skills that both soothe and align with the kind of life the client wants to build.
body_md: Rather than listing coping skills purely by how calming they are, have the client also rate how well each one fits the life they are trying to build, a skill that isolates the client from people who matter might soothe short term while working against a value of connection. Keep the ones that score well on both. This produces a shorter, more genuinely useful menu than a generic list.

fields.label: A coping skill and how calming it is
How well it fits my values
Another skill and the same two ratings
A skill that scores well on both
A skill I might want to swap out

title: Phobia Exposure Distress Tolerance Card
summary: A skills card to use during a planned exposure to a feared object or situation.
goal: Give the client skills to stay with a planned exposure step instead of escaping it.
body_md: List two or three skills the client will use to stay present during a planned exposure step, paced breathing, a grounding phrase, reminding themselves the goal is staying rather than feeling calm. Rehearse the card before the actual exposure happens. Log distress at the start, peak and end of the step to show the client their own pattern of the fear settling over time.

fields.label: The exposure step planned
Skill I will use to stay with it
Distress at the start
Distress at the peak
Distress at the end

title: Partner Support During Exposure Sheet
summary: Defines exactly how a partner can help during a planned exposure without accidentally rescuing.
goal: Keep a well-meaning partner's support from turning into an escape route during exposure work.
body_md: A supporting partner's instinct to comfort can accidentally let the client escape the exposure early, so this spells out exactly what helpful support looks like, staying nearby, not offering an out, a specific phrase of encouragement, versus what to avoid. Both partners agree on the plan together before the exposure happens. Debrief afterward on what actually helped.

fields.label: Client: what support helps during exposure
Client: what accidentally lets me escape
Partner: what I will say or do
Partner: what I will avoid doing
How the last exposure went with this plan

title: Brave Steps Feared Thing Chart
summary: A child builds a step-by-step chart toward a feared object or situation, adding a sticker at each step.
goal: Give a child a visible, gradual path toward a feared thing instead of an all-or-nothing leap.
body_md: The parent and child break a feared thing, a dog, the dark, a doctor visit, into small steps and build a chart together, adding a sticker each time a step is managed. The parent stays close and matches the pace to the child rather than pushing to the next step before the current one feels steady. Celebrate every step, including ones that need repeating.

fields.label: The feared thing on my chart
The step I am working on
How scared I felt (small, medium, big)
The sticker I earned
The next step on my chart

title: Fear Fact Check Game
summary: Players sort statements about a feared object into facts and fear-driven exaggerations.
goal: Separate the real facts about a feared object from what fear has exaggerated.
body_md: Prepare a set of statements about a commonly feared object or situation, some accurate and some exaggerated by fear, and have players sort them while discussing why fear tends to distort in that particular direction. This works especially well in a group where members share the same or different phobias. Close with each player's own fear-driven exaggeration and its more accurate counterpart.

fields.label: A statement I correctly sorted as fact
A statement I correctly sorted as exaggeration
My own fear-driven exaggeration about my feared thing
A more accurate version of that same statement

title: Fear Hierarchy Refresh Sheet
summary: Revisits and updates an existing exposure hierarchy as steps become easier or new ones become relevant.
goal: Keep a fear hierarchy current instead of letting it go stale as progress happens.
body_md: A hierarchy built weeks ago often no longer matches where the client actually is, so this has the client re-rate each step's current distress level and add any new steps that have become relevant since. Steps that have dropped in distress can be marked complete, and steps that never got attempted can be reconsidered. This keeps exposure work matched to real, current progress.

fields.label: A step whose distress rating has changed
New distress rating for it
A step I have not attempted yet
A new step to add to the hierarchy
The next step to work on

title: Appearance Talk Reduction Log
summary: Tracks how often a client's day involves appearance-focused talk or thought, without judgment.
goal: Build awareness of how much daily attention appearance talk is actually taking up.
body_md: Have the client note, without judging the count, every time appearance came up in their own thinking or in conversation with others across a day. Awareness alone often starts to shift the habit before any active change is asked for. Use the log to spot one specific moment or conversation pattern worth working on directly.

fields.label: A moment appearance came up in my thinking today
A moment it came up in conversation
How many times total, roughly
A pattern I noticed across the week
One moment I want to work on changing

title: Body as Instrument Practice
summary: Practices describing the body by what it does and enables rather than by how it looks.
goal: Shift attention from appearance to function as a different, workable relationship with the body.
body_md: Have the client list what their body actually lets them do across a typical day, carrying groceries, hugging someone, walking somewhere they wanted to go, without any reference to appearance. This is a genuine shift in attention, not a trick to force positivity, and some days will feel easier than others. Revisit the list regularly rather than writing it once.

fields.label: Something my body let me do today
Another thing
A way my body has supported me over the years
How it felt to describe my body this way
What I want to notice more of tomorrow

title: Mirror Time Limit Practice
summary: Practices a brief, timed mirror check paired with a grounding skill instead of an open-ended one.
goal: Interrupt a pattern of extended mirror-checking with a bounded, skills-paired alternative.
body_md: Extended mirror-checking often increases distress rather than resolving it, so this sets a short time limit for any mirror check, thirty seconds works for many clients, followed immediately by a grounding or self-soothing skill. Log how often the urge to check longer showed up and how the paired skill affected it. This is a gradual practice and does not need to be perfect from day one.

The skill I paired with it
The urge to check longer, rated 0 to 10
How I felt right after using the skill
What I noticed by the end of the week

title: Partner Appearance Comment Agreement
summary: Has a couple agree on how appearance gets talked about, or not, between them.
goal: Give a couple a shared, explicit agreement about appearance comments instead of leaving it unspoken.
body_md: Well-meaning appearance comments, even compliments, can land badly for a partner working on their body image, so this has both partners name what kind of comments actually help, what kind do not, and agree on an alternative way to express care that does not center appearance at all. Revisit if either partner notices the agreement slipping. Keep the tone collaborative rather than restrictive.

Partner A: appearance comments that do not help
Partner B: appearance comments that help

title: Bodies Do Many Things Drawing
summary: A child draws themselves doing several favorite activities to connect their body to what it can do.
goal: Help a child build an early, function-focused relationship with their own body.
body_md: The parent and child draw the child doing a handful of favorite activities, climbing, dancing, drawing itself, and talk about what the body was doing in each picture rather than how it looked. This plants an early function-focused frame for body image before appearance-focused messages take hold more strongly. Keep the conversation light and led by what the child brings up.

fields.label: An activity I drew myself doing
What my body was doing in that picture
Another activity I drew
How my body helped me do it
My favorite thing my body lets me do

title: Focus Relay Race
summary: A group relay game that breaks a task into short, timed bursts with movement breaks between.
goal: Practice sustaining short bursts of focus with built-in movement as a reward.
body_md: Each round pairs a short, timed focus task, a quick puzzle or worksheet, with a burst of movement, a lap or a stretch relay, between rounds. Framing the movement as a built-in part of the game rather than a break earned by sitting still models a rhythm of focus and release that a client can later adapt on their own.

fields.label: How long I stayed focused during a round
What helped me stay with the task
What pulled my attention away
How the movement break felt afterward

title: Anniversary and Milestone Planning Sheet
summary: Plans in advance for an upcoming anniversary, holiday or milestone likely to bring grief to the surface.
goal: Reduce the shock of a grief spike by planning for a known difficult date in advance.
body_md: A known difficult date, an anniversary, a birthday, a first holiday without someone, tends to bring grief closer to the surface, and planning for it in advance softens the impact more than hoping it won't be that hard. Naming what kind of day the client wants, alone or with others, marking it or trying to move past it, and one support person to have on call, turns a dreaded date into something with a plan.

fields.label: The upcoming date and what it marks
What kind of day I want this to be
One way I want to mark or acknowledge it
A support person I'll have on call that day
What I'll do if it's harder than expected

title: Avoidance Pattern Spotter
summary: Tracks the small, everyday ways a client avoids a feared situation beyond the obvious ones.
goal: Help a client notice subtle avoidance that keeps a phobia maintained without them realizing it.
body_md: Avoidance isn't always as obvious as skipping the feared situation entirely; it often shows up in smaller ways, sitting near an exit, bringing a companion every time, checking obsessively before going. Logging these smaller patterns over a week usually reveals more avoidance than the client realized, which is useful information for planning the next exposure step.

fields.label: A small avoidance I noticed this week
What it let me skip or soften
How obvious or subtle it was
A step I could take to reduce this specific avoidance

title: New Parent Bingo
summary: A bingo card of common new-parent moments, normalizing the chaos through shared recognition.
goal: Normalize the messiness of early parenthood through shared, playful recognition.
body_md: Each square names a common new-parent moment, wearing yesterday's shirt, forgetting a name mid-sentence, and players mark a square when it has happened to them, calling bingo when a row fills in. The playful format takes some of the shame out of moments that can otherwise feel like private failures, since the room usually fills in the same squares together.

title: Long-Distance Connection Planner
summary: Plans concrete ways to maintain connection across distance or opposite schedules.
goal: Give a couple a deliberate structure for staying connected when time together is limited.
body_md: Distance or mismatched schedules do not have to mean drifting, but they do mean connection needs planning instead of happening by default. Naming a few small, repeatable rituals, a call at a set time, a shared show, a running text thread, gives the relationship something to lean on between the times they are together. Revisit it when the schedule changes.

fields.label: Partner A: what makes me feel connected even at a distance
Partner B: what makes me feel connected even at a distance
One ritual we'll try this week
How we'll handle it if one of us misses it

title: Digital Overwhelm Reset
summary: A short audit of notifications, screens and open tabs that are crowding out a client's attention.
goal: Help a client notice what digital habits are draining their focus and choose one change.
body_md: Most clients underestimate how much of their day is spent reacting to notifications rather than choosing where their attention goes. Walk through a typical day and mark where a screen interrupted something else, then pick one boundary to trial for a week: a phone charging outside the bedroom, one email check block, one app removed from the home screen. Revisit at the next session rather than expecting the change to stick on the first try.

What I was doing right before I picked up my phone
How I felt in my body in that moment

title: Life Role Transition Map
summary: Maps the roles a client is leaving, keeping and taking on during a major life change.
goal: Help a client name what a transition is asking them to give up and gain.
body_md: A transition like a new job, retirement, or children leaving home changes a client's day-to-day identity even when the change itself is wanted. Naming the roles that are ending, continuing and starting gives shape to an otherwise vague sense of unease and opens a conversation about which losses need acknowledging before the client can settle into what comes next.

fields.label: The role or routine I'm leaving behind
What I'll miss about it

title: Weekly Reset Ritual Planner
summary: Builds a short end-of-week routine for closing out unfinished business before rest.
goal: Give a client a repeatable way to transition out of a demanding week.
body_md: Some clients carry the week's unfinished tasks into the weekend because nothing marks the switch from doing to resting. A short, repeatable ritual, closing open tabs, writing tomorrow's first task, a specific place and activity, gives the mind a cue that it is safe to stop. The content matters less than the repetition; encourage the client to keep it short enough that they will actually do it.

fields.label: What usually keeps running in my head after the work week ends

What rest looks like once the ritual is done

title: Saying No Practice Sheet
summary: Gives a client scripted language for declining requests without over-explaining.
goal: Build a client's confidence in setting a limit without a guilt spiral afterward.
body_md: Clients who over-commit often believe a no needs an airtight justification, which turns every request into a negotiation. Practicing a short, warm decline, with no elaborate excuse attached, out loud in session before trying it in real life builds the muscle. Track what actually happens afterward; most clients find the fallout is smaller than the guilt predicted.

fields.label: A recent request I said yes to but wish I hadn't
A short way I could have declined it
What I'm afraid will happen if I say no
One request coming up this week I could practice on

title: Mental Filter Correction Sheet
summary: Catches the habit of dwelling on one negative detail while filtering out the rest.
goal: Help a client notice when one bad moment is coloring their whole read of a day.
body_md: A client replaying one critical comment from a mostly good meeting is filtering out everything that went well. Logging the whole picture next to the detail that has stuck makes the imbalance visible without arguing the client out of the feeling. Over a few entries, a pattern usually appears: a specific type of moment the filter locks onto.

fields.label: The one detail that's stuck with me
What else actually happened, including what went fine or well
How much weight I've been giving the one detail, 0 to 10
A more complete way to describe the whole event

title: Black-and-White Thinking Scale
summary: Uses a 0-to-10 line to loosen an all-or-nothing read of a situation.
goal: Help a client find the middle ground their thinking has skipped over.
body_md: A client stuck in all-or-nothing language, a total failure, a complete disaster, rarely has room to notice partial outcomes. Drawing a 0-to-10 line and marking where the situation actually falls, then naming what sits at the far ends for comparison, gives the client's own words something to measure against. This works best with a concrete recent example rather than a hypothetical one.

fields.label: The all-or-nothing statement I caught myself thinking
What a true 0, the worst version, would look like
What a true 10, the best version, would look like
Where the actual situation falls on that line
What that number tells me that the original statement missed

title: Readiness to Change Ruler
summary: Scores how important, confident and ready a client feels toward a specific change.
goal: Locate where a client's ambivalence actually sits before setting a goal.
body_md: Pushing a client toward action before they are ready usually backfires into resistance. Scoring importance, confidence and readiness separately on a 0-to-10 scale, then asking why the number is not lower, often surfaces the client's own reasons for change rather than the clinician's. Low confidence with high importance points toward a skills gap rather than a motivation problem.

fields.label: The change I'm considering
How important this feels right now, 0 to 10
How confident I am I could do it, 0 to 10
Why that number and not one lower
What would need to be true for the number to go up

title: Should Statements Rewrite Sheet
summary: Trades a rigid should statement for a more flexible, self-chosen version.
goal: Loosen the guilt and pressure that rigid rules create.
body_md: Should statements, about the self or other people, carry a hidden rule that rarely survives being said out loud. Writing the rule down, asking where it came from, and rewriting it as a preference rather than a demand takes some of the moral weight out of falling short. Watch for the client applying the same rigid rule to someone else in the room without noticing.

fields.label: A should statement I catch myself using often
Where I think this rule came from
What happens, in my body or mood, when I break it
A more flexible version of the same idea
How that flexible version feels to say out loud

title: Mind Reading Check Sheet
summary: Separates what a client assumed someone else was thinking from what was actually said.
goal: Show a client how often they are reacting to a guess rather than a fact.
body_md: A client who is sure they know what someone else is thinking is usually reacting to their own guess rather than any evidence. Logging the assumed thought next to what the other person actually said or did creates a small, repeatable check. Over several entries the client can start running this check in real time instead of after the fact.

fields.label: What I assumed the other person was thinking
What they actually said or did
How I reacted based on my assumption
What I might ask instead of assuming next time

title: Values vs Rules Sort
summary: Sorts a client's stated goals into ones chosen from values and ones inherited as rules.
goal: Help a client tell the difference between what they want and what they think they should want.
body_md: Clients often carry a long list of goals without noticing that some come from a felt sense of what matters and others come from an old rule about what a good person does. Sorting a list of goals into these two piles, and sitting with the discomfort of a goal that turns out to be someone else's rule, opens room for the client to choose deliberately rather than by default.

fields.label: A goal or standard I hold myself to
Where this came from, if I trace it back
Does this feel chosen or inherited
If chosen, what value is underneath it
If inherited, do I want to keep it

title: Present-Moment Senses Practice
summary: A brief five-senses noticing exercise to anchor a client in the current moment.
goal: Give a client a portable way to step out of their head and into the room.
body_md: This is a simple noticing practice rather than a way to make discomfort disappear; a client who expects to feel calm afterward may be disappointed and disengage. Frame it instead as a way to widen attention beyond whatever thought has been looping, one sense at a time, without judging what is noticed. It travels well: a waiting room, a car, a hallway before a hard meeting.

fields.label: Something I can see right now
Something I can hear right now
Something I can feel touching my skin right now
Something I can smell right now
What shifted, if anything, after noticing all four

title: Unwelcome Guest Metaphor
summary: Uses the image of an uninvited houseguest to practice making room for a difficult feeling.
goal: Help a client stop spending energy trying to evict a feeling that keeps coming back.
body_md: Ask the client to picture the feeling as a houseguest who showed up without an invitation and will not be argued out the door. Fighting the guest, or pretending they are not there, tends to make the visit longer and louder. Practicing instead setting them a chair and going on with the evening gives the client language for acceptance that does not require liking the feeling.

fields.label: The feeling I've been trying hardest to get rid of
What I usually do to try to evict it
What happens when I do that
What it might look like to set this feeling a chair instead
What I could still do with the guest in the room

title: Committed Action Obstacle Map
summary: Maps the internal and external obstacles standing between a client and a values-based step.
goal: Help a client plan around obstacles instead of being surprised by them.
body_md: A values-based goal often stalls at the first obstacle because the client had not planned for it as a normal part of the path rather than a sign to stop. Naming the likely internal obstacles, a thought, a feeling, an urge to quit, next to the external ones gives the client a map instead of a surprise, and a line for what they will do when each one shows up.

fields.label: The values-based step I want to take
An internal obstacle likely to show up, a thought or feeling
What I'll do when it shows up
An external obstacle likely to show up
What I'll do when that shows up
The very next small step, regardless of obstacles

title: Thoughts on a Cloud Practice
summary: A brief defusion exercise picturing thoughts drifting past like clouds rather than facts.
goal: Give a client practice watching a thought instead of being pulled into it.
body_md: Ask the client to notice a thought, place it on an imagined cloud, and watch it drift rather than chase it or push it away. The point is not to empty the mind but to practice the small shift from being inside a thought to watching it pass. Some clients find it easier with eyes open, tracking real clouds or ceiling tiles as the visual anchor.

fields.label: A thought that's been looping today
What it felt like to place it on the cloud and watch it drift
A thought that was hard to let drift
What I noticed in my body during the practice

title: One-Mindfully in the Moment Practice
summary: Practices doing one thing at a time with full attention, the one-mindfully mindfulness skill.
goal: Reduce the split attention that keeps a client half-present in daily tasks.
body_md: Pick one routine task, washing a dish, walking to the car, and practice giving it full attention instead of the usual multitasking. Clients often notice how quickly the mind wanders back to planning or replaying; the skill is in noticing the wander and returning, not preventing it. Building this in low-stakes moments makes it more available during a harder one.

fields.label: The task I chose to practice on
How many times I noticed my mind wander
What it wandered to
What doing the task fully felt like compared to usual

title: Interpersonal Effectiveness Warm-Up Script
summary: A short, low-stakes script for practicing an interpersonal effectiveness skill before it is needed for real.
goal: Build fluency with an assertive script before a client needs it under pressure.
body_md: Skills that sound clear on paper often disappear under real pressure because the client has never said the words out loud. Picking a low-stakes upcoming interaction, returning an item, asking a coworker a small favor, and rehearsing the actual sentences in session builds the muscle memory before a higher-stakes conversation needs it.

fields.label: A low-stakes interaction coming up this week
What I want to ask for or say
The exact opening line I'll use
How I'll stay steady if the other person pushes back

title: Distress Tolerance Skills Menu
summary: A personalized list of distress tolerance skills a client can reach for in an overwhelming moment.
goal: Give a client a ready reference for getting through intense distress without making it worse.
body_md: Distress tolerance skills exist to get a client through an intense moment, not to fix the problem underneath it. Building a short, personalized list in session, ranked by what has actually worked before, means the client is not inventing a plan while already overwhelmed. Keep it somewhere physically accessible; a list saved only in memory tends to disappear exactly when it is needed.

fields.label: A distress tolerance skill that's worked for me before
A second skill I want to try
Where I'll keep this list
A recent moment this list would have helped

title: Shared Calendar Sync Meeting
summary: A short weekly meeting structure for keeping two schedules and responsibilities visible to both partners.
goal: Reduce the friction that comes from one partner tracking everything alone.
body_md: Invisible logistical labor, remembering appointments, deadlines, whose turn it is, tends to fall on one partner by default and quietly breeds resentment. A short standing meeting where both partners bring their calendars and divide the coming week's load out loud makes the labor visible and shared rather than assumed. Keep it brief and practical; save the emotional conversations for another time.

fields.label: Partner A: what's on my plate this week
Partner B: what's on my plate this week
What we're splitting and how
One thing that fell through the cracks last week and why

title: Conflict Cool-Down Signal System
summary: Sets up a shared, agreed-on signal for either partner to call a pause during an escalating conflict.
goal: Give both partners a way to interrupt escalation before it does damage.
body_md: Once a conflict is escalating, either partner trying to reason their way out often makes it worse. Agreeing in advance, outside of conflict, on a specific word or gesture either partner can use to call a pause, and what happens during the pause, turns a heated moment into something both partners already have a plan for. The signal only works if both partners agreed to honor it before it was needed.

fields.label: Partner A: a moment I wished we'd had a way to pause
Partner B: a moment I wished we'd had a way to pause
The signal we're agreeing on

How we'll come back together afterward

title: Vulnerability Sharing Circle
summary: A structured turn-taking exercise for sharing something each partner rarely says out loud.
goal: Deepen intimacy by practicing vulnerability in a low-risk, structured format.
body_md: Vulnerability is easier to practice with structure than to ask for cold. Each partner takes a turn sharing something true and rarely spoken, a worry, a hope, a regret, while the other partner only listens and reflects back what they heard before responding. Keep the prompts open enough that either partner can choose how deep to go.

fields.label: Partner A: something true I rarely say out loud
Partner B: what I heard, reflected back
Partner B: something true I rarely say out loud
Partner A: what I heard, reflected back
What it felt like to be the one listening

title: Team Family Chore Chart
summary: A visual chart where a child picks and tracks age-appropriate chores as part of the household team.
goal: Build a child's sense of contribution and follow-through with a concrete, visible system.
body_md: The parent and child pick a short list of age-appropriate tasks together, then the child marks each one off as it is done, ideally with a sticker or check rather than a grade. Keep the tone collaborative rather than transactional; the point is a felt sense of contributing to the household, not a reward economy. Adjust the list together every few weeks.

fields.label: The chores I picked for this week
Which ones I finished today
One I found hardest and why
How I felt when I finished the list

title: Morning Mood Check Wheel
summary: A spinning wheel a child turns each morning to name how they're arriving to the day.
goal: Build a child's early vocabulary for naming feelings before the day gets going.
body_md: The child decorates and turns a simple paper wheel with faces or colors each morning, landing on however they are feeling that day. The parent's job is to receive the answer without trying to fix or talk the child out of it, just to acknowledge it and note anything that might need extra patience that day. Over a few weeks, patterns tied to certain days or events often become visible.

fields.label: What my wheel landed on this morning
One word for why I feel that way
Something that might help today
How my wheel felt different from yesterday's

title: Gratitude Garden Craft
summary: A child adds a paper flower to a growing garden for each thing they're grateful for.
goal: Build a child's habit of noticing good things with a hands-on, growing visual.
body_md: The parent keeps a poster or paper garden bed on the wall, and the child adds a decorated paper flower each day naming something they are grateful for, however small. The visible growth of the garden over weeks does more of the work than the individual entries; let the child choose colors and decorations freely rather than steering the content.

fields.label: What flower I'm adding today
Why I picked that thing
How many flowers are in my garden now
My favorite flower so far and why

title: New Sibling Adjustment Storybook
summary: A child builds a simple illustrated storybook about becoming a big sibling.
goal: Give a child a hands-on way to process the changes a new sibling brings.
body_md: A new baby reshapes an older child's routines and attention even in a loving household, and a storybook the child controls gives them somewhere to put mixed feelings without needing the words for them yet. The parent helps with the pages but lets the child choose what happens in the story, including a page for a hard feeling if one comes up; that page deserves the same warm reception as any other.

fields.label: The title of my storybook
A page about what changed at home
A page about a feeling I've had, even a hard one
A page about something I like about being a big sibling
How I want the story to end

title: Story Chain Circle Game
summary: A group builds one story together, each person adding a sentence in turn.
goal: Build group cohesion and flexible thinking through shared, low-stakes creativity.
body_md: Sitting or standing in a circle, each group member adds one sentence to a story that has no set direction, building on whatever the last person said rather than steering it themselves. The rule is no vetoing another player's addition, only building on it, which practices flexibility and tolerating a story that does not go the way any one person planned. Debrief by asking what was hard about not being in control of the story.

fields.label: A sentence I contributed that I liked
A moment the story went somewhere I didn't expect
How it felt to build on someone else's idea instead of my own
What this reminds me of in real life

title: Would You Rather: Boundaries Edition
summary: A card game of paired scenarios that gets a group talking about setting limits.
goal: Open group discussion about boundaries through low-stakes, playful choices.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a card with two boundary-related scenarios, would you rather tell a friend no or do something you don't want to do, and picking one, then briefly saying why. The paired-choice format lowers the stakes of talking about a topic that can otherwise feel exposing, and the debrief afterward is where the real conversation about each player's own boundaries usually opens up.

fields.label: A card I drew and what I picked
Why I picked that one
A scenario I found genuinely hard to choose between
One boundary of my own this game reminded me of

title: Pass the Feeling Ball
summary: A group passes a ball around, naming a feeling and a time they felt it before passing it on.
goal: Build group comfort naming a range of feelings out loud.
body_md: Sitting in a circle, each player holds the ball, names a feeling, a brief moment they felt it, and passes it on to the next person. No feeling can repeat once it has been said, which gently pushes the group past the same few words toward a wider feelings vocabulary. Keep the shared moments brief and let any player pass on details if they would rather not elaborate.

fields.label: The feeling I named
A brief moment I felt it
A feeling someone else named that I don't use often
How it felt to hear the group's different feelings

title: Values Tug of War Game
summary: A verbal tug-of-war where two sides argue for competing values in a shared scenario.
goal: Make the tension between competing values felt and discussable rather than abstract.
body_md: Give the group a scenario with two values pulling in different directions, honesty versus loyalty, ambition versus rest, and split into two sides to argue for each value before swapping. Making the pull between two genuinely good things visible, rather than framing one side as simply wrong, helps players recognize the same tension in their own decisions. Debrief on which value usually wins for each player and why.

fields.label: The scenario and two values in tension
The side I argued and my strongest point
The strongest point I heard from the other side
Which value tends to win for me in real life

title: Circle of Support Web Game
summary: A group passes a ball of yarn to build a visible web representing their support connections.
goal: Make a group's sense of connection and support visible and felt.
body_md: Holding one end of a ball of yarn, a player names someone who supports them and tosses the ball to another player, who does the same, building a visible web across the circle. The web makes an otherwise abstract idea, that support exists even when it does not feel that way, into something the group can see and hold. Debrief by asking what it felt like to be named by someone else.

fields.label: Someone I named as support and why
What it felt like when someone named me
A gap in the web I noticed for myself
One strand of the web I want to strengthen

title: Comfort Corner Building Craft
summary: A child builds a physical calm corner with objects that help them feel safe and settled.
goal: Give a child a concrete, physical place to return to when they feel unsettled.
body_md: The parent and child choose a small corner or box and fill it together with a few comforting objects, a soft blanket, a favorite toy, a drawing, that the child picks themselves. This stays a resource for calming and safety, not a place to revisit what happened; keep the conversation on what helps the child feel settled now. If a child discloses anything concerning while building it, the clinician's reporting duties apply as they would in any session.

fields.label: The corner or box I picked
Objects I put in it and why
How I feel when I go there
Who helped me build it

title: Grounding Skills Card Draw Game
summary: A group or individual draws cards and practices a different grounding skill on each turn.
goal: Build familiarity with a range of grounding skills through low-stakes repetition.
body_md: Each card names a different grounding skill, naming five things seen, pressing feet into the floor, holding something cold, and the player practices it for a minute before rating how settled they felt out of ten. Playing it outside of a distressed moment builds familiarity so the skill is easier to reach for when it is actually needed. Keep this game to grounding skills only; it is not a place to process what happened.

fields.label: A skill I drew and how it felt
How settled I felt after, 0 to 10
The skill that worked best for me today

title: Pacing Plan for Hard Days
summary: Helps a client plan how to pace activity and rest on days when trauma symptoms are stronger.
goal: Give a client a plan for getting through a harder day without pushing past their capacity.
body_md: Some days carry more activation than others, and pushing through on those days the same way a client would on a calmer one often backfires. Naming early signs that today is a harder day, and a short list of adjustments, fewer commitments, more breaks, a support person on call, turns a reactive scramble into something planned in advance. Review and adjust the plan after it has been tried once.

fields.label: An early sign today is a harder day
One commitment I could lighten or postpone
A support person I could reach out to
A pacing adjustment that's worked before

title: Present-Day Evidence Scan
summary: A brief scan for current, present-day evidence of safety when a trauma reminder triggers alarm.
goal: Help a client's nervous system catch up to the fact that the threat has passed.
body_md: A trauma reminder can trigger a full alarm response even when nothing in the current moment is actually dangerous. Scanning the room for concrete, present-day evidence, the date, the people nearby, the locked door, gives the client's thinking mind something to offer the alarmed body. This works alongside grounding rather than instead of it, and is meant for the present moment, not for reviewing the past event.

fields.label: What triggered the alarm feeling
The year and place I actually am right now
Someone or something nearby that's safe

title: TIPP for Trauma Reminders
summary: Applies the TIPP distress tolerance skill to the spike that follows a trauma reminder.
goal: Give a client a fast, body-based way to bring down an activation spike.
body_md: When a reminder sends the body into a full activation spike, thinking-based skills are often out of reach until the body calms down first. TIPP, temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing, paired muscle relaxation, works on the body directly and can bring the spike down enough for other skills to become usable again. Rehearse which TIPP option the client has access to before it is needed.

fields.label: The TIPP option most available to me, cold water, movement, breathing, or muscle relaxation
How activated I felt before, 0 to 10
How activated I felt after, 0 to 10

title: Supporting Without Reassuring Sheet
summary: Helps a couple find ways to support anxiety that don't feed a reassurance-seeking cycle.
goal: Give both partners a plan for support that doesn't accidentally maintain the anxiety.
body_md: A partner's constant reassurance often feels like the kind thing to do but can quietly keep an anxious cycle going, since the relief never lasts and the question comes back. Naming a few alternative responses together, sitting with the worry instead of answering it, a hug instead of a fact, a shared decision on how many times to answer the same question, gives both partners a plan they have agreed on rather than an in-the-moment guess.

fields.label: Anxious partner: what reassurance I tend to ask for
Supporting partner: what I usually say or do
What tends to happen after the reassurance wears off
An alternative response we want to try

title: What-If Spiral Interrupter
summary: Catches a chain of what-if worries and finds the first link where the chain could be interrupted.
goal: Help a client interrupt a worry spiral earlier instead of riding it to the end.
body_md: A what-if spiral rarely announces itself; by the time a client notices, they are several links deep into an imagined worst case. Writing out the whole chain after the fact, from the first what-if to the last, shows the client where the spiral usually starts, which is often a much smaller and more manageable thought than where it ends up. Practice catching the chain at that earlier link next time.

fields.label: The first what-if in the chain
The next few links, one after another
Where the chain ended up

title: Anxious Body Signals Log
summary: Tracks the earliest physical signs anxiety is building, before the worry thoughts catch up.
goal: Help a client catch anxiety earlier by tracking body signals instead of waiting for the thoughts.
body_md: The body often signals rising anxiety, a tight chest, a clenched jaw, restless legs, before the client consciously registers worry thoughts. Logging these signals across a few days builds a personal early-warning list, so a regulation skill can be used earlier, when it is easier for the body to settle, rather than waiting until the worry is already in full swing.

fields.label: A physical signal I noticed today
What was happening around that time
How high the anxiety got, 0 to 10

title: Worry Toss Bean Bag Game
summary: Players toss a bean bag into labeled bins representing different-sized worries and discuss where their own worries land.
goal: Build a playful, shared vocabulary for sorting the size of a worry.
body_md: Set up bins labeled small, medium and big worry, and each player tosses a bean bag, names a worry that fits that size, and briefly says why. The physical sorting makes an abstract skill, judging how big a worry actually is, into something concrete and shared, and hearing other players sort their own worries often helps a player recalibrate their own.

fields.label: A worry I sorted and which bin it landed in
Why I sorted it that way

title: Energy Cost Ledger
summary: Tracks which daily activities cost energy and which return it, to guide low-energy planning.
goal: Help a client plan a day around their actual energy rather than an idealized one.
body_md: Low mood often narrows a client's sense of what is worth doing to almost nothing, which makes planning feel pointless. Logging a handful of daily activities as either costing or returning energy, regardless of how small, builds a personal map the client can use to balance a low-energy day instead of guessing. The point is not to avoid every costly activity, just to know the trade before making it.

fields.label: An activity from today that cost me energy

title: Small Values Step Finder
summary: Finds the smallest possible step toward a value when energy and motivation are low.
goal: Keep a client moving toward what matters even when a full step feels out of reach.
body_md: Waiting for motivation before acting rarely works with low mood, since motivation tends to follow action rather than precede it. Naming a value, then scaling the step down until it feels almost too small to count, a two-minute version of the task, gives the client something achievable today rather than an all-or-nothing goal that gets postponed again.

fields.label: A value I want to move toward

title: Behavioral Activation Ladder Card

goal: Give a client an ordered starting point when everything feels equally impossible.
body_md: When everything feels equally hard, a client often ends up doing nothing rather than choosing where to start. Ranking a short list of activities from easiest to hardest gives an ordered starting point; the goal on a low day is simply the next rung up, not the top of the ladder. Revisit the ranking often, since it shifts with mood.

title: Small Sparks Jar

goal: Help a child notice small moments of interest without pressure to feel fully happy.
body_md: The child adds a small drawing to the jar for anything that gave even a flicker of interest, not full happiness, which keeps the bar low enough to actually reach on a hard day. The parent's role is to notice the jar filling without pushing for a bigger reaction than the child has; a slow week is worth naming too, without alarm.

title: What Matters Right Now Check
summary: A brief check-in on which task actually connects to a client's values before switching tasks.
goal: Help a client choose the next task deliberately instead of chasing whatever feels urgent.
body_md: Attention often follows whatever feels most urgent or interesting in the moment, which can pull a client away from what actually matters to them. A brief pause before switching tasks, naming which option connects to a value and which is just noise, gives the client a moment of choice rather than autopilot. This works better as a quick habit than a long planning session.

fields.label: The task pulling my attention right now

title: Task Switching Cost Log

goal: Make the hidden cost of task-switching visible so a client can plan around it.
body_md: Switching tasks feels free in the moment but usually costs real time re-orienting to whatever was interrupted. Logging a few switches across a day, what pulled attention away and how long it took to get back on track, makes an invisible cost visible, which often motivates small changes like closing tabs or setting a timer before a task even more than being told to focus does.

title: Task Reminder Without Nagging Agreement
summary: A couple agrees on a neutral way to remind each other about tasks that doesn't feel like nagging.
goal: Reduce the resentment cycle that builds around reminders and forgotten tasks.
body_md: A reminder can land as nagging even when it is meant kindly, and the partner doing the reminding often feels unheard when it is dismissed. Agreeing together on a neutral format, a shared list, a specific phrase, a set time of day, takes the tone out of the reminder and puts the system in charge instead of either partner. title: External Memory System Setup Sheet

goal: Reduce reliance on memory alone by building a trusted external system.
body_md: Relying on memory alone to track tasks sets a client up to feel like they are failing at something that is not really a memory problem at all. Choosing one place, a single app, a wall calendar, a notebook, and building the habit of writing everything there the moment it comes up takes the load off memory and puts it somewhere trustworthy and checkable.

title: Supporting Recovery Without Policing Sheet

goal: Give both partners a way to support recovery that doesn't erode trust or autonomy.
body_md: A supporting partner who takes on constant monitoring, checking, searching, questioning, often does it out of fear, but it tends to erode trust on both sides rather than reduce urges. Naming together what support actually looks like, and what crosses into policing, gives both partners a clearer, more sustainable role than vigilance alone.

title: Urge Wave Tracker for Teens

goal: Help a teen see that an urge to use a substance rises and falls rather than lasting forever.
body_md: The teen draws a simple wave shape each time an urge shows up, marking how strong it felt at the peak and how long it took to come back down, with a trusted adult checking in afterward rather than during. Seeing the wave shape across several entries helps a teen trust that an urge passes on its own, which is easier to believe on paper than in the moment.

title: Urge Surfing With TIPP Combo Card
summary: Pairs the urge surfing skill with a TIPP option for when an urge feels too intense to simply observe.
goal: Give a client a backup plan for when an urge is too intense to ride out through observation alone.
body_md: Urge surfing works by observing the urge rise and fall rather than acting on it, but some urges arrive too intense for observation alone to hold. Pairing it with a fast body-based TIPP option, cold water, brief intense movement, gives the client a way to bring the intensity down first, then return to surfing the rest of the wave.

title: Cravings and Consequences Card Game
summary: A group card game matching common urge triggers to a range of coping responses.
goal: Build quick recall of coping responses to common urge triggers through repetition.
body_md: Players draw a trigger card, a stressful call, a certain place, a certain person, and match it to a coping response card from a shared pile, discussing whether the match would actually work for them. Playing it in a group normalizes that triggers are common and specific rather than a personal failing, and the discussion surfaces coping options a player might not have thought of alone.

title: Values Beyond the Next Urge Practice
summary: Connects a client's urge-surfing practice to a specific value they're protecting by riding it out.
goal: Give a client a reason to ride out an urge that's bigger than willpower alone.
body_md: Riding out an urge on willpower alone tends to run out; connecting the choice to a specific value, being present for a child, trusting oneself, keeping a job, gives the moment a reason that outlasts the urge itself. Naming the value before the urge hits, not during, means it is already available when the moment gets hard.

fields.label: A value that matters more to me than giving into this urge

title: Anger as Information Practice
summary: Reframes an anger episode as information about a boundary or value rather than a problem to suppress.
goal: Help a client use anger as a signal instead of fighting or acting on it automatically.
body_md: Anger often carries information, a crossed boundary, a violated value, that gets lost when the client either suppresses it or acts on it immediately. Slowing down to ask what the anger might be pointing to, separately from deciding what to do about it, gives the client room to respond deliberately instead of reactively. This is not about excusing harmful behavior, just about listening to the signal first.

body_md: Between an irritating event and a full anger response sits a thought, often about fairness, disrespect or intention, that does the escalating. Logging that specific thought next to the event shows the client where their own interpretation, not just the event, is driving the intensity, which opens room to question whether the interpretation is the only possible one.

body_md: Teams answer trivia-style questions about physical warning signs of rising anger and matching cool-down skills, scoring points for correct answers and bonus points for sharing a real example from their own life. The competitive format keeps a topic that can feel heavy light enough to engage with, while the shared examples build a group's collective toolkit.

body_md: A lot of anger runs through a belief that something is unfair, which can be true and still benefit from a second look before acting on it. Writing out the fairness belief, then considering what the other person might say about the same situation, does not require agreeing with them, just widening the picture enough to choose a response rather than react on the first read.

goal: Prevent repair attempts from backfiring by timing them to when both partners are ready.
body_md: A repair attempt offered before a partner has cooled down can land as pressure and restart the conflict instead of ending it. Agreeing in advance on a rough signal for when each partner is ready, a specific amount of time, a physical cue, gives both partners permission to wait without it meaning the issue is being avoided.

body_md: The pull to resolve uncertainty through a compulsion is strong precisely because it works in the short term. Logging moments the client sat with not-knowing instead, even briefly, and what happened afterward, builds a personal record that uncertainty is survivable, which counts for more than being told so directly.

body_md: A delay period on its own can feel like an empty wait that makes the urge harder to resist. Pairing the delay with an active distress tolerance skill, a cold object, paced breathing, brief movement, gives the client something to do with the wait rather than just enduring it, which tends to make the delay easier to hold.

body_md: A partner answering reassurance questions over and over often feels like the caring thing to do but tends to keep the cycle going, since the relief never lasts. Agreeing together on a limited, warm response, one answer and then a gentle redirect, gives the supporting partner a way to stay kind without feeding the cycle, and gives the other partner a predictable, less punishing boundary.

Hearing other players do the same normalizes the discomfort of uncertainty and builds a shared vocabulary for tolerating it.

Externalizing the urge as a character the child can argue with, rather than a part of themselves, makes it easier to resist without shame. Keep the tone playful and the parent involved as a coach, not a judge.

goal: Help a teen see a panic episode as something that rises and falls rather than something dangerous.
body_md: After a panic episode has passed, the teen draws its shape as a wave, marking the peak and how long it took to settle, with a trusted adult available to talk it through afterward rather than during. Seeing the shape on paper across a few episodes helps a teen trust the pattern: it rises, it peaks, it comes back down, every time.

body_md: Teams sort statements, panic can make you faint, a racing heart during panic is dangerous, into fact or myth, then discuss what is actually happening in the body during a panic wave. Correcting scary misunderstandings in a low-stakes group setting tends to land better than a one-on-one lecture, since players hear the same reassurance from a teammate's own experience too.

body_md: Filling this out during a panic episode is not the goal; it is meant for afterward, once things have settled, so the client can build pattern recognition without adding pressure in the moment itself. Over several entries, common precedents, poor sleep, a specific place, skipped meals, tend to surface, giving the client something concrete to plan around.

goal: Reduce the fight against panic sensations that tends to prolong them.
body_md: Fighting panic sensations, trying to make them stop immediately, often keeps the alarm system activated longer than letting the wave run its natural course. A short card the client can read during an episode, reminding them the sensations are uncomfortable but not dangerous and will pass on their own, practices willingness instead of struggle. Rehearse this outside of an episode first.

body_md: A panic spike is a body event first, which means a body-based skill often works faster than a thinking-based one in the first minute. Pairing a splash of cold water or a cold object held to the face with slow, extended exhales gives the client a fast, reliable combination to reach for, and rehearsing it calm makes it easier to access when panic actually hits.

title: Parent Assumption Check Sheet

body_md: A parent's first read of a child's behavior, they are doing this on purpose, they don't respect me, often narrows the response before other explanations get considered. Writing out the assumption next to a few other possible reasons for the same behavior, tiredness, a skill the child hasn't learned yet, a need not being met, gives the parent more than one way to respond.

goal: Build a family's shared, comfortable vocabulary for naming feelings.
body_md: Each family member takes a turn acting out a feeling without words while the rest guess, then briefly shares a recent moment they felt that way. Parents modeling their own feelings in the game, including harder ones like frustration, gives children permission to do the same, and the shared laughter tends to lower the guard around a topic families often avoid.

body_md: Most parents can describe the kind of parent they want to be, but that description tends to disappear exactly when a predictable trigger, bedtime, a meltdown in public, hits. Naming the value in advance, and one concrete way to act on it in that specific moment, gives the parent something to reach for when the pressure is on, rather than reflecting only after the fact.

body_md: Children notice quickly when parents disagree on discipline, and inconsistency between two adults tends to create more conflict than either approach alone would. Comparing each parent's instinct on a few common scenarios, then agreeing on one shared approach for each, gives a child consistency and takes a recurring argument off the table between the parents.

Keep the focus on noticing rather than earning a reward; the map is meant to build a felt sense of being a person who makes good choices, not a transaction.

Make room for the child to mention a harder feeling too, less attention, a new routine, and receive it as calmly as the excited parts.

Writing both side by side, without judging either one, usually reveals that the expectation was never realistic to begin with, which takes some of the self-blame out of an ordinary hard day.

body_md: Severe sleep deprivation affects judgment the way any other vulnerability factor does, which makes it a poor condition for big decisions, quitting something, a major purchase, a relationship ultimatum. Building a simple rule, delay any decision above a certain size until after a real stretch of sleep, protects the new parent from choices made under conditions they wouldn't trust for anyone else.

Naming a few values or interests that predate the baby, and one small, realistic way to touch one of them this week, does not compete with parenting; it protects a fuller sense of self alongside it.

Listing qualities and relationships that stay true regardless of a recent mistake or win, being someone people trust, being curious, being kind, gives the client a more stable place to stand than the next performance.

body_md: The parent and child name a few of the child's strengths together, kind, brave, funny, good at building things, and the child draws or paints a symbol for each on a simple fabric or paper cape. Wearing the finished cape gives the child a playful, physical reminder they can return to, and the parent can reference a symbol on a hard day rather than a lecture.

Writing the guilty thought down, then what information and choices were actually available in that moment, separates hindsight from what was realistically possible, which does not erase the grief but can loosen the guilt.

How settled I felt after, 0 to 10
A skill I want to use more
Where I'll remember to use it

title: Reclaiming Small Choices Practice
summary: Practices noticing and making small everyday choices to rebuild a client's sense of agency.
goal: Rebuild a client's felt sense of choice and agency through small, present-day decisions.
body_md: Rebuilding a sense of agency often starts small: noticing and deliberately making choices, what to eat, what to wear, how to spend a free hour, that are entirely the client's own. This is not about the size of the choice but the felt sense of choosing it; tracking a few across a week can build evidence of agency that words alone do not provide.

fields.label: A small choice I made today, entirely my own
How it felt to make that choice on purpose
Another small choice I want to make this week
What noticing these choices is building for me

title: Grounding Through the Senses Card
summary: A five-senses grounding card for moments when a client feels unsafe in the present moment.
goal: Give a client a fast, reliable way to return to present-moment safety.
body_md: When a feeling of unsafety surfaces without a present-day cause, orienting deliberately to the five senses can help the body catch up to the fact that the current moment is safe. This card is for use in the moment, naming what's seen, heard, felt, smelled and, if appropriate, tasted, and is meant to support safety and grounding, not to explore what happened.

fields.label: What I can see right now
What I can hear right now
What I can feel touching my skin right now
What I can smell right now
How settled I feel now, compared to before

title: My Body, My Say Poster
summary: A child decorates a poster naming the trusted adults they can tell if something feels wrong.
goal: Reinforce a child's sense that their body belongs to them and who they can tell if that isn't respected.
body_md: The parent and child name a short list of trusted adults, drawn or written on a poster, the child can go to if anything ever feels wrong or confusing about their body or safety. Keep the language simple and reassuring rather than frightening, and let the child ask questions at their own pace. As with any tool for children, a disclosure during this activity carries the clinician's usual reporting duties.

fields.label: The trusted adults I named
What I can say if something feels wrong
Where I'll keep this poster
A question I still have

title: Supporting a Partner's Pace Agreement
summary: Helps a couple agree on physical and emotional intimacy moving at the survivor partner's pace.
goal: Give a couple a shared, explicit agreement about pacing intimacy around a survivor partner's needs.
body_md: A supporting partner's good intentions can still move faster than a survivor partner's actual readiness, especially around physical closeness. Naming a clear, revisitable agreement, what pace feels right, what check-in language either partner can use, how the survivor partner can pause without it being taken personally, gives both partners something explicit to work from rather than guessing.

fields.label: Survivor partner: what pace feels right for me right now
Supporting partner: what I want to understand about that pace
The check-in language we're agreeing on
How the survivor partner can pause without it being taken personally

title: Couple Coping Skills Inventory
summary: Each partner shares which coping skills actually work for them so the other can support, not guess.
goal: Help partners support each other's coping with informed help instead of guessing.
body_md: A well-meaning partner often reaches for whatever coping method works for them, which may be exactly wrong for the other. Each partner names a short, honest inventory of what actually helps them cope, and what doesn't, however that compares to what the other partner assumed, gives both a more accurate map to work from during a hard moment.

fields.label: Partner A: what actually helps me cope
Partner A: what doesn't help, even if well-meant
Partner B: what actually helps me cope
Partner B: what doesn't help, even if well-meant

title: Coping Skill Rotation Card
summary: Tracks which coping skills are overused or underused to keep a client's toolkit balanced.
goal: Prevent a client from relying on the same one or two coping skills to the exclusion of others.
body_md: Clients often default to the same one or two coping skills, which can work fine until that skill isn't available or stops being enough on its own. Logging which skill was used each time, over a couple of weeks, shows the client their own pattern and makes room to deliberately practice an underused skill before it is needed under pressure.

fields.label: The coping skill I used today
How well it worked, 0 to 10

title: Coping Skill Matching Thoughts Sheet
summary: Matches a coping skill to the specific kind of thought or feeling driving distress in the moment.
goal: Help a client choose a coping skill that fits the actual problem, not just habit.
body_md: Not every coping skill fits every kind of distress: a grounding skill helps a racing body more than a spiraling thought, and a thought-challenging skill helps a spiraling thought more than a racing body. Naming what is actually driving the distress in the moment, body or thoughts, before picking a skill increases the odds the chosen skill actually helps.

fields.label: What's driving the distress right now, body or thoughts
A skill that matches a racing body
A skill that matches spiraling thoughts

title: Coping Skills Cost of Avoidance Sheet
summary: Compares the short-term relief of an avoidant coping habit to its longer-term cost.
goal: Help a client see the trade-off in a coping habit that offers relief now but costs more later.
body_md: A coping habit that offers real relief in the moment, scrolling, sleeping through a problem, avoiding a hard task, can still cost more over time than it gives back. Writing the short-term benefit next to the longer-term cost, honestly and without judgment, does not demand the client give up the habit immediately, just see the full trade they are actually making.

fields.label: The coping habit I'm looking at
What it gives me in the short term
What it costs me over the longer term
A coping skill that might give some of the same relief at less cost

title: Willingness Over Certainty Ladder
summary: Reframes exposure steps around a client's willingness to feel fear rather than certainty they won't.
goal: Shift a client's exposure practice from seeking certainty to practicing willingness.
body_md: Waiting to feel certain the feared thing won't happen before taking a step keeps a client stuck, since the certainty they are waiting for rarely arrives. Reframing each step on the ladder around willingness to feel the fear, rather than a guarantee of safety, lets the client move even while afraid, which is what actually builds the new pattern.

fields.label: The feared situation
A step on the ladder I could take this week
What certainty I've been waiting for that isn't coming
What I'm willing to feel in order to take the step anyway

title: Fear Ladder Trivia Challenge
summary: A trivia game testing knowledge of common fear responses and matching approach strategies.
goal: Build shared, playful knowledge of how exposure and fear responses actually work.
body_md: Teams answer trivia questions about how fear responses work, why avoidance keeps fear alive, what happens to fear with repeated approach, scoring bonus points for sharing a personal example. Making the mechanics of fear into a shared, playful challenge tends to demystify it more effectively than a straightforward explanation alone.

fields.label: A trivia question I answered

A personal example I shared

title: Exposure Support Without Rescuing Sheet
summary: Helps a couple agree on support during exposure practice that doesn't accidentally rescue from the fear.
goal: Give a couple a shared plan for exposure support that builds rather than undermines progress.
body_md: A supporting partner who steps in the moment fear rises, taking over, offering an escape, can unintentionally undo the value of an exposure step. Agreeing in advance on what support looks like, staying present without taking over, a specific phrase of encouragement, gives both partners a plan that respects the process instead of shortcutting it out of care.

fields.label: Partner practicing exposure: what support actually helps

title: Feared Outcome Prediction Sheet
summary: Records a client's predicted worst outcome before an exposure step, then compares it to what happens.
goal: Build evidence against a phobia's predicted catastrophe through repeated real-world comparison.
body_md: A phobia usually comes with a specific predicted catastrophe attached to the feared object or situation. Writing the exact prediction down before an exposure step, then what actually happened afterward, builds a growing, personal record that the predicted outcome doesn't match reality, which does more than reassurance alone.

fields.label: The exposure step I'm about to take

title: Body Gratitude Circle Game
summary: A group takes turns naming something their body lets them do, building a function-focused conversation.
goal: Build a group's shared, function-focused way of talking about the body.
body_md: Going around the circle, each player names one thing their body lets them do, run, hug someone, taste their favorite food, rather than how it looks. Keeping the conversation strictly function-focused models a different way of relating to the body than the appearance-focused talk most players are used to, and hearing a range of answers widens what counts as worth appreciating.

fields.label: What I named my body lets me do
Something someone else named that I hadn't thought of

title: Appearance Comment Urge Surfing Card
summary: Applies urge surfing to the urge to comment critically on one's own appearance out loud.
goal: Help a client ride out the urge to voice a critical appearance comment instead of acting on it.
body_md: The urge to say a critical comment about appearance out loud, in a mirror, getting dressed, in a photo, often passes on its own if given a moment, the same way any other urge does. Noticing the urge rise, riding it out without saying the comment or its opposite, and noticing it fall builds practice separating the urge from the action.

fields.label: The urge I noticed

title: Appearance-Free Compliment Practice
summary: A couple practices giving each other compliments that have nothing to do with appearance.
goal: Build a couple's habit of affirming each other in ways not tied to how they look.
body_md: Compliments that default to appearance, even kind ones, can reinforce the idea that looks are the primary thing worth noticing about a partner. Practicing a round of compliments that are entirely about something else, a quality, an effort, a moment of kindness, builds a habit of affirming a partner as a whole person rather than primarily how they look.

fields.label: Partner A: a non-appearance compliment for my partner
Partner B: a non-appearance compliment for my partner

title: My Body Can Do Anything Drawing
summary: A child draws themselves doing something they're proud their body can do.
goal: Build a child's early function-focused relationship with their body.
body_md: The child draws a picture of themselves doing something they are proud their body lets them do, climbing, dancing, riding a bike, and the parent asks about what the body was doing rather than how it looked in the picture. Keeping the conversation on ability and effort plants an early frame that resists the appearance-focused messages a child will encounter later.

fields.label: What I drew myself doing

title: Body Talk Awareness Log
summary: Tracks how often a client hears or engages in appearance-focused talk across a day.
goal: Build a client's awareness of how much everyday talk centers on appearance.
body_md: Appearance-focused talk is so common it often goes unnoticed, which makes it hard for a client to see how much of their day is shaped by it. Logging a few moments across a day, a comment overheard, a thought about how something looked, a compliment given, builds awareness of the pattern, which is usually the first step toward choosing a different kind of conversation.

fields.label: A moment I noticed appearance-focused talk today
Where it came from, myself or someone else

title: Mistake Monster Craft
summary: A child builds a friendly monster that eats mistakes and turns them into something learned.
goal: Give a child a playful way to separate a mistake from being a bad kid.
body_md: The parent helps the child build a simple monster from paper or a box with an opening for a mouth, then the two of them write small mistakes on slips of paper and feed them to the monster, saying out loud one thing the mistake taught. Keep the monster somewhere visible so a real mistake later in the week has somewhere to go right away. The parent naming their own mistakes for the monster helps too.

fields.label: A mistake I want to feed the monster

How I feel after

title: Listening Ears Headband Craft
summary: A child decorates a headband with big paper ears to practice noticing what good listening feels like.
goal: Make the abstract skill of listening something a child can put on and practice.
body_md: The child decorates a simple headband with oversized paper ears, then wears it during a short listening game where the parent tells a brief story and the child repeats back one detail. Talk about what good listening looks like in the body: eyes, stillness, not planning what to say next. Use the headband again during a moment the child is having trouble listening, as a playful reset rather than a correction.

fields.label: A detail I remembered from the story
What my body was doing while I listened well
What made listening harder at other times
When I want to wear my listening ears again

title: Growth Mindset Garden Craft
summary: A child plants paper flowers that grow each time they try something hard, whether or not it works.
goal: Teach a child that effort on a hard thing counts, separate from the result.
body_md: The child draws or cuts out a paper flower for a garden poster each time they try something that felt hard, whatever the outcome, and the parent writes a short note of what was attempted next to it. A flower for an attempt that did not work out yet belongs in the garden just as much as one for a success. Look at the growing garden together at the end of the week and notice how full it got.
