goal: Use it to help partners talk about how differently each of them grieves.
body_md: Each partner says how they grieve, what helps and what they need from the other. Normalize different paces and styles. Agree on one way to be close in grief and one way to give each other space.

fields.label: Partner A: how I grieve
Partner B: how I grieve
What we each need
A way to be close
A way to give space

title: Relationship Interpretation Check
summary: A sheet for checking a first reading of a partner's behavior against other explanations.
goal: Use it to help a client test a first reading of a partner's behavior against other possibilities.
body_md: Ask for a recent moment and the story the client told. List two other explanations and one thing they could ask. Rate belief in each. It does not excuse harm, so leave room for it if the pattern is real.

fields.label: What my partner did
What I told myself it meant
Two other possible explanations
A question I could ask

title: GIVE and FAST Skills Practice
summary: A practice sheet for using GIVE to keep the relationship and FAST to keep self-respect.
goal: Use it to help a client balance keeping a relationship with keeping their self-respect.
body_md: Pick a real interaction and plan it using GIVE (gentle, interested, validate, easy manner) and FAST (fair, apologies, stick to values, truthful). Role-play a first line. Look at which matters most in this situation.

fields.label: The interaction
What I will do for GIVE
What I will do for FAST
What matters most here

title: Repair Attempt Phrases Card
summary: A card of phrases partners can use to stop an argument from escalating.
goal: Use it to help partners choose repair phrases they can say mid-argument.
body_md: Each partner picks phrases that would help them and agrees to accept the other's attempts. Practice saying them in session. Notice how each one hears them. Attempts fail when they sound sarcastic, so check the tone.

fields.label: Partner A: phrases that would help me
Partner B: phrases that would help me
How we will signal a repair
How we will accept it

title: Perspective Swap Game
summary: Players argue a fictional disagreement from each side, then swap.
goal: Use it to help players practice seeing a disagreement from the other person's side.
body_md: Pairs get a fictional disagreement and argue one side for two minutes, then swap sides. Debrief what each felt, and what they understood about the other side. Keep it fictional so nobody has to argue their own conflict.

fields.label: The side I argued first
What I understood when I swapped
What I would say differently
What I will take into my own relationships

title: Personal Safety Circle Sheet
summary: A sheet for mapping who is close, who is safe and who is not.
goal: Use it to help a client map who feels safe and who does not.
body_md: Draw circles and have the client place people by how safe they feel. Nothing about events is needed. Discuss support and how to protect time and space. If risk to safety appears, follow your own process and your reporting duties.

fields.label: People in my safest circle
People I keep at a distance
What makes someone feel safe
One way I can protect my space

title: Self-Soothing Kit Builder
summary: A builder for a kit of comforting items for each sense.
goal: Use it to help a client collect comforting items for hard moments.
body_md: Choose one item per sense and keep them in a box. Try each in session. The kit is about comfort and pacing. If distress is high, use grounding first. Include 988 (call or text) on the list of supports and complete it in session.

fields.label: Something to see
Something to hear
Something to touch
Something to smell or taste
A support I can contact, including 988

title: Intimacy Pacing and Consent Agreement
summary: A page where partners agree how to go slowly and check in about closeness.
goal: Use it to help partners agree on pacing, choice and check-ins about closeness.
body_md: The partner who is a survivor says what pace and signals feel right, and the other listens and repeats. Both are free to say stop at any point. Agree on a signal and a way to reconnect afterward. No detail of the past is needed.

fields.label: Partner A: what pace feels right
Partner B: what I will do to support it
Our stop signal
How we will reconnect afterward

title: Body Boundaries Traffic Light Craft
summary: Children make a traffic light to sort touches and situations they like and do not like.
goal: Use it to help a child practice saying no and telling a trusted adult.
body_md: The child colors a traffic light and places examples such as high fives and hugs on green, yellow and red. The parent shows they will listen if the child tells them anything. Remember your reporting duties if a child discloses.

fields.label: A touch I like
A touch I do not like
What I can say
Who I can tell if something feels wrong

title: Coping Skill Trial and Review Sheet
summary: A sheet for trying a skill in real life and reviewing how it worked.
goal: Use it to help a client test a skill in real life and note what happened.
body_md: Pick one skill and ask the client when they will try it. Afterward, they rate how it felt and what helped or got in the way. Keep the sheet simple so it gets used.

fields.label: The skill
When I tried it
What happened
What helped or got in the way

title: Coping Thoughts Card Builder
summary: A builder for cards holding helpful coping statements the client believes.
goal: Use it to help a client write coping statements they find credible.
body_md: Ask the client to write statements in their own voice, such as "this is hard and I have handled hard things". Reject statements they do not believe. Rehearse them and place the cards where they will be seen.

fields.label: A hard moment I face
A statement I would believe in that moment
How much I believe it (0 to 100)
Where I will keep the card

title: ACCEPTS Distraction Menu
summary: A menu of distraction ideas sorted by activities, contributing, comparisons, emotions, push away, thoughts and sensations.
goal: Use it to help a client build a personal list of distractions for high-distress times.
body_md: Walk through each letter and ask the client to write one idea that would work for them. Emphasize that distraction is a short-term skill for getting through a peak, not for avoiding everything. Star three.

fields.label: An activity
Something I could do for someone else
An emotion I could invite instead
A sensation I could use
My three favorites

title: Coping That Fits My Values Sort
summary: A sort of coping habits by whether they move a client toward or away from what matters.
goal: Use it to help a client sort coping habits by the direction they move them.
body_md: Write coping habits on cards. The client sorts them into toward and away from what they value. Many habits do both; note the mix. Choose one to do more and one to do less.

fields.label: A coping habit I use
Does it move me toward or away from what I value?
What it gives me
One I want to do more of

title: Coping Skills Spinner Craft
summary: Children make a spinner with coping skills and spin to try one.
goal: Use it to give a child a playful way to pick and practice a coping skill.
body_md: The child decorates a paper plate spinner with six skills, such as breathing, drawing, or asking for a hug. Spin and try the one it lands on. The parent tries one, too. Post it somewhere handy.

fields.label: A skill on my spinner
When I could use it
How it felt
A skill I would add

title: Fear Rating and Avoidance Record
summary: A record of fear ratings and avoided situations over time.
goal: Use it to help a client track fear levels and what they avoid, so planning is concrete.
duration: Five minutes daily for a week
body_md: The client records each time they met or avoided a feared thing, their fear from 0 to 100, and what they did. Use it as a baseline for planning steps. Review it without judgment, since avoidance makes sense.

fields.label: The feared thing and the situation
My fear (0 to 100)
What I did
What I avoided and what it cost me

title: Feared Outcome Checking Sheet
summary: A sheet for writing what the client expects and checking it against what happened.
goal: Use it to help a client compare the feared outcome with what happened in an exposure step.
body_md: Before a step, the client writes the feared outcome and how sure they are. After, they write what happened. Look at the gap. If the outcome was unpleasant but manageable, note the coping. Repeat with the next step.

fields.label: The step I am about to take
What I expect will happen
What happened
What I learned

title: Fear Ladder Willing Hands Practice
summary: A practice of standing with open hands and willing posture while facing a feared step.
goal: Use it to help a client approach a feared step with a willing body posture.
body_md: Teach willing hands (palms up, relaxed) and a half-smile as body cues that support approach. Practice with a mild step in session. Ask what changes in the body. This is a cue, not a guarantee.

fields.label: The step I am facing
What my body does when I face it
What willing hands felt like
What I will try next

title: Exposure Coach Role Agreement
summary: A page where a partner agrees to support without pushing or rescuing.
goal: Use it to help partners agree how one coaches the other through exposure steps.
body_md: The partner facing the fear says what support looks like and how they want to be encouraged. The partner says what they can and cannot do. Agree on what happens if the step is too much. Coaching is not rescuing or pushing.

fields.label: Partner A: how I want to be supported
Partner B: what I can do
What we will say when it gets hard
How we will end a step

title: Body Image Values Sort
summary: A sort of what a client wants their relationship with their body to stand for.
goal: Use it to help a client name values for how they relate to their body.
body_md: Offer values such as respect, curiosity, ease and care, and have the client choose three. Ask what an action based on each would look like on an ordinary day. Keep the focus on how they relate to themselves and steer clear of anything about size or shape.

fields.label: Three values for how I treat my body
An action that fits each
A moment I did it this week
A barrier to it

title: Appearance Thoughts Record
summary: A record of thoughts about appearance and the situations that bring them up.
goal: Use it to help a client see the thoughts and situations that raise body worries.
body_md: Ask for a situation, the thought and the mood. Look at the rules and comparisons hiding in the thought. Write a balanced alternative that does not depend on appearance. Steer clear of measuring or rating the body.

fields.label: The situation
The thought about my appearance
How I felt
A balanced thought that is not about looks

title: Kind Body Care Plan
summary: A plan for caring for the body out of respect, not punishment.
goal: Use it to help a client choose acts of care for their body that come from kindness.
body_md: Ask the client to list ways of caring for their body, such as rest, stretching, a warm bath. Choose two for the week. Notice whether they come from care or from a should. Adjust the list to fit.

fields.label: A way I can care for my body
Why it matters to me
When I will do it
How it felt

title: Partner Affirmation Exchange
summary: A page where partners share what they appreciate about each other as whole people.
goal: Use it to help partners share appreciation for each other that goes beyond appearance.
body_md: Each partner writes and says three things they appreciate that are not about looks. The listener says thank you without deflecting. Discuss how the other partner hears comments about bodies and agree on ones to skip.

fields.label: Partner A: what I appreciate about you
Partner B: what I appreciate about you
How it felt to hear
Comments we agree to skip

title: Body Neutral Statements Game
summary: Players turn appearance statements into neutral or function-based ones.
goal: Use it to help players practice neutral, function-based ways to talk about the body.
body_md: Prepare cards with appearance-focused comments. Players rewrite each into neutral or function-based language such as "my legs carry me". Debrief how it felt. Avoid any statements about size, shape or eating.

fields.label: A comment I rewrote
How I rewrote it
How the new one felt
Where I could use it

title: Eulogy Values Exercise
summary: Invites the client to imagine how they hope to be remembered, then turns it into values.
goal: Surface values the client cares about most through a longer view.
body_md: Some clients find this moving and some find it heavy, so offer it as an imagined exercise and let them pace it. Keep the focus on qualities and actions rather than achievements, and stay with the client if grief surfaces. If a client mentions hopelessness or wanting to die, stop and follow your own risk process, and complete this in session rather than as homework.

fields.label: What I hope people would say about how I treated them
What I hope they would say I stood for
Qualities I want to be known for
Where my life today matches this
Where my life today does not match this
One small action this week that moves toward it
If this brings up thoughts of harming myself, I can call or text 988 right away

title: Energy Drain and Refill Inventory
summary: Sorts daily activities and people into those that drain and those that restore the client's energy.
goal: Show the client where energy actually goes and what refills it.
body_md: Ask for real examples from the past two weeks rather than general beliefs. Some items will land in both columns, and that is useful to talk about. Look for one drain that can be trimmed and one refill that can be scheduled, and keep the plan small enough to try this week.

fields.label: Activities or people that left me drained
Activities or people that left me refilled
Something that surprised me about these lists
A drain I could shorten, share or say no to
A refill I could add this week
When exactly I will do it
What might get in the way

title: Change Landing Plan
summary: Maps a big life change into what stays steady, what shifts and what support is needed.
goal: Help the client steady themselves through a move, job change or other transition.
body_md: Start with what will stay the same, since clients in transition tend to focus only on loss or uncertainty. Then sort the changes into ones they can shape and ones they can only respond to. Review the support list together and check that each person on it has actually been asked.

fields.label: The change that is happening
What will stay the same
What is ending or shifting
Parts of this I can shape
Parts I can only respond to
Small routines I will protect
People I will tell and lean on
One thing I am looking forward to

title: Specific Gratitude Log
summary: Builds a habit of noticing one specific good thing each day and what made it possible.
goal: Move gratitude from general statements to specific, noticed moments.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Specific beats general here, so prompt for details of the moment instead of a list of big things. Clients who find gratitude forced can start with neutral or small moments. Review the log together and look for patterns in people, places and times of day.

fields.label: Today's good thing in one sentence
Where I was and who was there
What I noticed in my body or mood
What made it possible
Who I could thank or tell
A pattern I see across the week

title: Nighttime Settling Checklist
summary: A step-by-step evening checklist that gives the body and mind cues of present-day safety before sleep.
goal: Support steadier nights through a predictable, grounding routine.
body_md: Build the checklist together in session and keep it short enough to do when tired. Include checking the room, a grounding step and a comforting sensory cue. It aims to stabilize, so never ask for details of what happened. If nights stay hard, talk through next steps and other supports together.

fields.label: What I will do to check my room feels safe
A grounding step I will use in bed
A comforting sound, scent or texture I will keep close
What I will say to myself if I wake up
Someone or something I can reach for if a night is hard
How the night went and what helped

title: Circle of Control Sort
summary: Sorts worries into what the client can control, influence or only accept.
goal: Direct worry energy toward what can be acted on.
body_md: Ask for current worries, not hypothetical ones, and sort them together in three rings. Expect the outer ring to be fullest. The point is to pair each outer-ring worry with a way to ride it out, and each inner-ring worry with one action this week.

fields.label: Worries on my mind this week
Ones I can control directly
Ones I can only influence
Ones I can do nothing about
One action I will take on a controllable worry
How I will let an uncontrollable worry pass
What I notice after sorting

title: Energy-Matched Task Sorter
summary: Sorts tasks by how much energy they need so low-mood days still include something doable.
goal: Help the client match tasks to energy instead of waiting to feel better.
body_md: Use it when the client says they can do nothing or everything is too big. Sort tasks into low, medium and high energy and plan which go with which kind of day. Celebrate low-energy wins. Keep your own judgment about whether more support is needed alongside it.

fields.label: Tasks I need to do
Tasks that take very little energy
Tasks that take medium energy
Tasks that take a lot of energy
What I will do on a low-energy day
What I will do on a better day
How I felt after doing one task

title: Free Time Fill Plan
summary: Plans how to use the hours when substance use used to happen, with real alternatives.
goal: Prepare for empty time and the urges that come with it.
body_md: Ask the client to name the specific times of day or week when substance use most often happened and what filled them. Plan alternatives that are actually available and appealing, not just virtuous. Review what got used and what flopped, and adjust together without judgment.

fields.label: Times when I used to use substances
What I was doing or feeling then
What I will do in that time now
Who I can contact at those times
Something enjoyable I can look forward to
What I will do if an urge shows up anyway
What I will change after this week

title: Anger Needs Behind the Heat
summary: Helps the client name the need, hurt or worry beneath an angry reaction.
goal: Connect anger to the need underneath so it can be voiced differently.
body_md: Use a recent event the client can still recall without being flooded, and do it after the heat has passed. Ask what was at stake for them. Many clients have few words for hurt or worry, so offer a short list of feeling words. End with how they could ask for the need directly.

fields.label: What happened
What I did or said
What I felt right before the anger
What mattered to me in that moment
The need I was trying to protect
How I could ask for it without the heat
What I would like to try next time

title: Places and Panic Avoidance Map
summary: Charts the places and situations the client avoids because of panic and what the avoiding costs.
goal: Show how avoidance has narrowed daily life and pick a first step back.
body_md: Draw the map together with home at the center and mark the places that feel harder. Ask what has been given up, since the costs often matter more to the client than the fear itself. Choose one place with modest difficulty and plan an approach with a helper and an exit plan they agree to.

fields.label: Places and situations I avoid
What I worry will happen there
What I have stopped doing because of it
Who or what helps me feel safer
One place I could approach first
What I will do if panic rises
What I learned after trying it

title: Weekly Connection Planner for Parents
summary: Plans small, specific moments of connection with a child across the week.
goal: Make connection a planned part of the week, not a leftover.
body_md: Keep the plan realistic for the family's schedule, because ten minutes that happens beats an hour that does not. Ask the parent what their child enjoys now, not what they used to. Review which moments worked and what the child said or did in response.

fields.label: Something my child enjoys right now
One moment this week I can give them my full attention
When and where it will happen
What I will put away or pause
A way I will show interest without correcting
What happened and how they responded
What I would like to repeat

title: Visitor and Help Boundaries Plan
summary: Helps new parents decide who visits, when, and what kind of help is actually wanted.
goal: Give the client a way to welcome useful help and pace the rest.
body_md: Many new parents feel they cannot say no to visitors or cannot ask for what would help. Go through each person and role-play a kind, short response. Encourage specific requests such as a meal or a nap. Watch for guilt, and keep the plan flexible as needs change.

fields.label: People who want to visit or help
What would truly help me right now
What would not help right now
How I will ask for the help I want
A kind sentence for saying not yet
Who I will tell first
What I will do if I feel overwhelmed

title: Small Talk Opener Bank
summary: Collects easy openers and follow-up questions the client can try in low-stakes settings.
goal: Give the client ready words for starting and keeping a conversation going.
body_md: Practice the openers aloud in session before assigning them. Start with low-stakes settings like a cashier or neighbor. Remind the client that a short, imperfect exchange still counts as practice. Afterward, compare what they predicted with what happened.

fields.label: Places where I could try a short chat
Three openers I am willing to say
A follow-up question I could ask
What I predict will happen
What I will do if the chat is short
What actually happened
What I will try next

title: Grief Energy Pacing Sheet
summary: Plans a week around limited energy during grief, balancing rest, tasks and connection.
goal: Keep the week manageable while grief takes up energy.
body_md: Grief can be tiring in ways clients do not expect, and they often judge themselves for doing less. Normalize reduced capacity and help them choose what is essential. Include one gentle way to feel connected and one rest period each day. Revisit as energy changes.

fields.label: What has felt most tiring lately
What must get done this week
What can wait or be shared
How I will rest each day
Someone I would like to spend time with
Something that brings me comfort
How I will be kind to myself on a hard day

title: Safe and Steady Daily Anchors
summary: Lists small daily anchors that help the client feel steady, in control and supported.
goal: Build predictable, stabilizing routines that support safety day to day.
body_md: Keep the focus on the present and on what helps the client feel steady, and do not ask for any details of the past. Let the client choose the anchors and the pace. If a step feels uncomfortable, adjust it or drop it. Check what they felt in their body as they practiced.

fields.label: A morning anchor I can count on
A place or object that helps me feel safe
A grounding step I can use during the day
A person I can check in with
An evening anchor before bed
What I noticed when I used an anchor
What I want to change or drop

title: Coping Reminder Placement Plan
summary: Decides where, when and how coping skills will be cued in the client's daily life.
goal: Put coping skills where the client will actually see them when stress hits.
body_md: Skills fail most often because they are not remembered in the moment. Choose two or three cues such as a phone reminder, a card in a wallet or a note on the bathroom mirror. Test the cues for a week and swap any that blend into the background.

fields.label: Coping skills I want to remember
Moments I most need them
Where I could place a reminder
A phone or alarm cue I could set
A person who could remind me
Which cue I noticed this week
What I will change

title: Avoidance Workarounds Inventory
summary: Lists the small workarounds a client uses to dodge a feared thing and what each costs.
goal: Make quiet avoidance visible so the client can choose where to loosen it.
body_md: Workarounds such as taking longer routes or asking someone else to do it are easy to miss because they feel sensible. List them without criticism and rate how much each costs in time, money or freedom. Choose one to loosen first and plan a support person.

fields.label: The feared thing or situation
Workarounds I use to avoid it
What each workaround costs me
What I am afraid would happen without it
The workaround I will loosen first
Who will support me
What happened when I tried

title: Homework Obstacle Forecast
summary: Links what was learned in session to one concrete task in the week ahead.
goal: Carry a session insight into daily life with a specific, small plan.
body_md: Fill it in together during the last ten minutes. Push for one task with a day and place attached, and ask the client to name what might get in the way. Open the next session with it, since review signals that between-session work matters.

fields.label: The main idea I am taking from today
One thing I will try this week
The day, time and place I will do it
What might get in the way
What I will do if that happens
How I will notice if it helped

title: Thought Challenging Flashcards
summary: Turns a practiced balanced thought into a pocket card to read at the moment it is needed.
goal: Make the balanced response easy to reach when the old thought is loud.
body_md: Build the card from a thought record the client has already completed, not from scratch. Keep the balanced statement in words the client would believe on a hard day. Have them rate belief in it before and after a read-through, and revise the wording if the rating stays low.

fields.label: The upsetting thought, as it sounds in my head
How strongly I believe it, 0 to 100
The facts that do not fit that thought
A balanced thought I can believe
How strongly I believe the balanced thought, 0 to 100
Where I will keep the card so I can reach it

title: Activity Barrier Problem-Solving Sheet
summary: Finds the specific obstacle behind a skipped planned activity and tests a workaround.
goal: Keep activity plans moving by solving the barrier rather than blaming motivation.
body_md: Use it when a planned activity was missed. Treat the miss as information about a practical or thought-based barrier, and help the client pick the smallest workaround to try. Watch for self-blame showing up as an explanation, and name it gently.

fields.label: The activity I planned and did not do
What was going on right before I skipped it
The thought that made it feel too hard
A smaller version I could do
Something or someone that could make it easier
When I will try the smaller version

title: Feelings Are Not Facts Check
summary: Separates how something feels from what the situation actually shows.
goal: Help the client notice emotional reasoning and look at the facts separately.
body_md: Pick a moment when a strong feeling was taken as proof, such as feeling like a failure. Have the client write the feeling and the facts in separate places so the gap is visible. Expect some pushback; the aim is to hold both, not to argue the feeling away.

fields.label: The feeling I had, and how strong it was
What the feeling told me was true
Facts that support that
Facts that do not fit it
What I might say to myself if I kept both
What I would do differently with that view

title: Grounding Skills Rehearsal Card
summary: Lets a client practice a chosen grounding skill while calm, then plan where to use it.
goal: Build a reliable grounding habit before it is needed.
body_md: Run it in session while the client is calm and stay with present-day practice only; it does not ask for any account of what happened. Let the client pick the skill that feels safest, rehearse it together, and adjust pacing if anything stirs up distress. Stop and ground if needed.

fields.label: The grounding skill I chose
What I notice in my body when I practice it calm
Where I could use it this week
Signs that tell me I need it
What I will say to myself while I use it
Who I could tell that I am practicing

title: Task Start Ritual Plan
summary: Builds a short, repeatable routine for getting started on a task that keeps getting put off.
goal: Lower the barrier to starting by making the first minutes automatic.
body_md: Choose one task that matters to the client and design the first two minutes in detail, including where to sit and what to open. Keep it small enough to feel almost silly. Check in next session on whether the ritual was used, not whether the task finished.

fields.label: The task I keep putting off
What gets in the way right at the start
My first two-minute action
Where and when I will do it
What I will tell myself when I want to delay
A reward or signal that I started

title: High-Risk Situation Rehearsal Plan
summary: Walks through an upcoming situation where substance use urges are likely and rehearses responses.
goal: Prepare specific responses for urges before a risky situation arrives.
body_md: Choose a real upcoming situation in the next week or two and rehearse it in session, including the moment an offer or urge appears. Let the client name the plan; your role is to ask what could go wrong with it. Keep the tone practical and free of blame.

fields.label: The situation coming up
Who or what will be there
Urges I expect, and when they may peak
What I will say or do in that moment
Who I can contact if the urge gets strong
How I will leave or change plans if I need to
What I will do afterward

title: Anger Aftermath Repair Sheet
summary: Guides a client through what to do after an angry episode, from calming down to repair.
goal: Turn the aftermath of anger into a step toward repair.
body_md: Use it after a recent episode once the client is calm, not in the heat of it. Keep the focus on what the client can own and what repair looks like, without making the client wrong as a person. Note the thoughts that kept the anger going for next time.

fields.label: What happened, in a sentence or two
The thought that fed my anger most
What I did that I wish I had done differently
What I want the other person to know
A repair step I can take, and when
What I will do sooner next time

title: Panic Avoidance Ladder
summary: Ranks places and activities a client avoids for fear of panic, from easiest to hardest.
goal: Plan gradual return to avoided places and activities.
body_md: Build the ladder with the client and rate each step for expected fear. Start with a step they rate about moderate so practice stays manageable, and plan to repeat it until fear falls before moving up. Check on safety behaviors that can creep back in.

fields.label: Places or activities I avoid because of panic
How anxious each one feels, 0 to 100
The easiest step I could practice first
What I am afraid will happen
Safety behaviors I might use, and how I will drop them
How I will know the step went well

title: Parent Expectation Check Sheet
summary: Helps a parent compare their expectations of a child with what is realistic for the child's age.
goal: Soften expectations that fuel parental frustration and guilt.
body_md: Use it with a parent who feels constantly let down by their child's behavior. Ask about the source of each expectation, often a family rule or an old belief about good parenting. Keep it supportive; parents often arrive feeling judged already.

fields.label: A moment this week when I felt frustrated
What I expected my child to do
Where I learned that expectation
What my child might be able to do at their age
A fairer expectation for next time
How I will tell my child what I need

title: Balanced Self-Appraisal Sheet
summary: Lists strengths and shortcomings side by side so a client can describe themselves fairly.
goal: Replace all-or-nothing self-ratings with a balanced, specific description.
body_md: Have the client fill in the strengths column first and accept only specific examples, not general claims. Expect the list of flaws to come easily and keep it to specifics too. The last prompt is the point: a fairer sentence the client would actually stand behind.

fields.label: A quality I like about myself, with an example
A quality I do not like, with an example
A time my shortcoming did not matter as much as I expected
What people who know me well might add
How I sum myself up now
A fairer way to sum myself up

title: Conversation Experiment Planner
summary: Sets up a small social experiment, such as asking a question, and records what actually happened.
goal: Test social fears with a planned, specific conversation.
body_md: Pick one small conversation the client can do this week and write the fear as a specific prediction. Ask the client to drop one safety behavior during it if ready. Review what actually happened, including what went better than expected.

fields.label: The conversation I will try
What I predict will happen
How sure I am, 0 to 100
One safety behavior I will try dropping
What actually happened
What I learned about my prediction

title: Grief Wave Coping Plan
summary: Helps a grieving client prepare for waves of feeling on hard days and dates.
goal: Plan ahead for hard moments so grief feels less like an ambush.
body_md: Ask about dates, places and moments that tend to bring a wave, and plan for them together. Let grief be grief; the plan is for support and pacing, not for getting rid of feeling. Include one thing the client can do for themselves and one person to reach.

fields.label: A day or moment I expect to be hard
What the wave usually feels like in my body
A thought that often comes with it
One thing that helps me get through it
A person I can reach out to
One way I can honor the person I lost

title: Safe Support Circle Plan
summary: Maps the people and places that feel safe and what a client wants from each.
goal: Strengthen present-day support and pacing for recovery.
body_md: Keep this about safety and support now; it never asks for any account of what happened. Let the client decide who goes on the map and what they want to share with each person, including nothing. Revisit it as trust changes. If the client is at risk, use 988 (call or text).

fields.label: A person or place where I feel safe
What I can ask of them
What I do not want to share yet
A sign that I need more support
A small step I can take to connect this week
What I will do if I feel unsafe

title: Coping Toolbox Match Sheet
summary: Matches specific coping skills to the situations and feelings they fit best.
goal: Choose the right coping skill for the moment instead of one for everything.
body_md: Have the client name three recent hard moments and pick a skill for each, noting whether it fit. Clients often rely on one tool and then call it useless when it fails. Highlight a mismatch as useful information, not a failure.

fields.label: A recent hard moment
What I felt, and how strong it was
The skill I used, if any
How well it fit, 0 to 10
A skill that might fit better
When I will try it next

title: Values Beyond Appearance Plan
summary: Connects a client's values to daily activities that do not depend on how they look.
goal: Shift attention and time from appearance toward what the client values.
body_md: Ask what the client would do with more time and attention if appearance mattered less, and build from their answer. Keep the plan concrete, with a day and a place. Do not debate how they look; redirect to what they value and what they want to do next.

fields.label: Something I value that has nothing to do with looks
A time I felt like myself
An activity I avoid because of how I feel about my appearance
A small step toward that activity
What I might tell myself when appearance thoughts show up
Who could do this with me

title: Hooked and Unhooked Log
summary: Tracks moments the client got pulled along by a thought or feeling, and the moment they noticed.
goal: Build the skill of noticing being hooked and choosing a next step.
body_md: Introduce hooks as anything that pulls a person away from what matters, with no moral weight on it. Ask for small, recent examples so the log stays light. The win is the noticing, however late, so celebrate a late catch as much as an early one, and look for the most common hook across the week.

fields.label: What was going on when I got hooked
What the hook was (a thought, a feeling, an urge to act)
What I did while hooked
The moment I noticed, and what told me
One small thing I could do next time to unhook
What I would rather be doing with this moment

title: Clean and Dirty Discomfort Sort
summary: Sorts a client's distress into the pain that comes with caring and the extra pain added by struggling.
goal: Separate unavoidable discomfort from the struggle layered on top of it.
body_md: Walk through one recent painful situation and sort each reaction into clean (the natural hurt) or dirty (what the fight against it added). Clients often file everything as dirty or everything as clean, so go slowly and let the client decide. It pairs well with willingness work afterward.

fields.label: A recent situation that hurt
The natural feelings that came up, the clean part
What I did to get rid of those feelings
What the struggle added, the dirty part
What it cost me to fight the feeling
What I could do with the clean part instead

title: Hexaflex Flexibility Snapshot
summary: A one-page picture of where a client feels flexible or stuck across the six ACT processes.
goal: Give client and clinician a shared map of where to focus next.
body_md: Use plain language for each of the six processes and have the client rate how free or stuck they feel in each one on a simple scale. It is a conversation starter rather than a score, and the ratings shift from week to week. Revisit it every few sessions to see what has moved.

fields.label: How free or stuck I feel with my thoughts, and an example
How willing I am to have hard feelings, and an example
How present I am in my day, and an example
How much I notice myself as more than my story
How clear I am on what matters to me
How much I act on what matters to me
The area I most want to work on first

title: Everyday Task Mindfulness Practice
summary: Turns one routine task into a daily practice of full attention and gentle returning.
goal: Practice present-moment contact inside ordinary life.
duration: Five minutes daily for one week
body_md: Pick a task the client already does, such as washing dishes or brushing teeth, and have them do it with full attention to sights, sounds and touch. The mind will wander, and each return is the practice. Watch for clients who turn it into a test they can fail.

fields.label: The task I chose
What I noticed with my senses
Where my mind went
How I brought my attention back
What was different about this task with my full attention
Another task I could try next

title: Sounds Around Me Anchor Practice
summary: A short listening exercise that helps a client stay in the present through what they can hear.
goal: Offer a steady, low-risk way to stay connected to the here and now.
body_md: Keep this brief and let the client keep their eyes open and stop at any time. Sounds in the room are a gentle entry point and need no talk about what happened. Practice in session first so it is familiar before the client tries it at home, and watch for any rise in distress.

fields.label: Sounds I can hear that are close to me
Sounds I can hear that are far away
One sound that feels neutral or pleasant
Where I feel steadier in my body while I listen
A place or time this week I could use this practice
Who or what reminds me I am here now

title: Worry Hands Defusion Exercise
summary: Uses the hands held over the eyes and then held away to show how thoughts pull focus.
goal: Let anxious clients feel the difference between fusing with worry and noticing it.
body_md: Have the client cover their face with their hands as if they were a worry and try to talk or look around, then lower them to the lap. Ask what changed. Many clients grasp defusion more from this than from explanation, so allow time to discuss, and run it with one real worry.

fields.label: A worry that shows up often
What it was like holding it up close
What it was like holding it at a distance
What I could still do with the worry in my lap
What matters to me that the worry gets in the way of
Where I could practice this in daily life

title: Values Reminder Sticky Notes Plan
summary: Places short values-based cues where a client with attention difficulties will meet them.
goal: Connect daily tasks to what matters so starting feels worth it.
body_md: Clients with attention challenges often know what to do but lose the why in the moment. Draft two or three short cues tied to real places such as a desk, a door or a phone. Keep the wording personal and change the cues when they become invisible.

fields.label: Something I keep putting off that matters to me
Why it matters, in a few words
A short cue I could write
Where I will place it so I see it
What I want to be doing when I see it
When I will change the cue to keep it fresh

title: Urge Bubble Watching Practice
summary: Pictures an urge as a bubble that rises, floats and pops, with a short log of what happened.
goal: Help clients ride out urges without acting on them.
body_md: Frame substance use urges as passing events the client can watch without acting. Practice in session with a mild urge before using it for stronger ones, and talk about the urge rising and falling. If urges feel overwhelming, return to your own safety plan and supports.

fields.label: The urge and what set it off
Where I noticed it in my body
What the bubble looked like as it grew
What happened as I watched it
How long it lasted
What I did next that fit what matters to me

title: Doubt Radio Practice
summary: Treats intrusive doubt as background radio the client can hear while still acting on values.
goal: Practice carrying doubt along instead of answering it.
body_md: Clients with intrusive thoughts often try to argue the radio into silence. Have them name the station, turn the volume down in imagination, and then do a chosen task. Avoid reassurance during the exercise, and expect the doubt to keep playing.

fields.label: What the doubt radio says
What I usually do to make it stop
What happens to the doubt when I do that
What I could do while the radio keeps playing
What matters to me that I am skipping
How it went when I let it play

title: Panic Welcome Mat Practice
summary: Practices welcoming panic sensations like a visitor rather than pushing them out.
goal: Shift a client's relationship with panic from fighting it to allowing it.
body_md: Start with a mild sensation in session and use a welcoming phrase such as 'here you are'. The aim is not to make the panic go away, which clients will try to use it for, so name that gently. Follow with a short debrief about what shifted.

fields.label: Sensations I notice when panic shows up
What I usually do to push them away
A welcoming phrase I could try
What happened when I let them be there
What I want to keep doing while they are there
When I will practice this again

title: Hooked Parent Reset Card
summary: A quick card for catching a parenting hook and returning to the parent the client wants to be.
goal: Give parents a short pause and values check in heated moments.
body_md: Have the parent name their typical hooks, such as thoughts of failing or urges to yell, and the parent they want to be in those moments. Keep the card small enough to live on a fridge or phone. Normalize that resets happen after the fact too.

fields.label: A moment I got hooked with my child
The thought or feeling that hooked me
What I did
The parent I want to be in that moment
A pause I could take, in a few words
One thing I could say or do next time

title: Worth Without Proof Practice
summary: Practices holding worth as a given rather than something to be earned or proven.
goal: Loosen the link between achievements and a person's sense of worth.
body_md: Clients with low self-esteem often collect evidence for and against themselves. Invite them to step out of the courtroom and ask what it would be like to treat worth as not up for debate. Expect resistance and go slowly.

fields.label: What I usually try to prove about myself
Who I am trying to prove it to
What it costs me to keep proving it
What I would do if my worth were not in question
A small action this week that fits that
What kind words I would say to a friend in my place

title: Willing in the Room Plan
summary: Plans a social situation around what the client is willing to feel rather than how to avoid it.
goal: Help clients move toward people while anxiety comes along.
body_md: Choose one small social step linked to something the client cares about. Ask what they are willing to feel to do it, and avoid promises that the anxiety will fade. Review afterward for what mattered, not how anxious they felt.

fields.label: A social step that matters to me
What I am afraid will happen
What I am willing to feel to do it
How I will bring my attention to the other person
What I will do if anxiety rises
How it went and what I learned

title: Relationship Hooks Noticing Sheet
summary: Helps a client spot the thoughts and urges that pull them into conflict or withdrawal with someone close.
goal: Notice relationship hooks early and choose a response that fits their values.
body_md: Use a recent, low-intensity exchange and trace the hook, the automatic response, and the alternative that fits the partner the client wants to be. Clients sometimes use it to prove the other person wrong, so keep it on their own behavior.

fields.label: A recent exchange that went badly
The thought or feeling that hooked me
What I did in response
What I would like my response to stand for
One different response I could try
How I could tell the other person what I am working on

title: Safe Now Anchor Phrases Sheet
summary: Builds a short set of present-tense phrases that remind a client where they are and that they have choices.
goal: Give the client a steady set of words for staying present.
body_md: Work in session, at the client's pace, and never ask for details of what happened. Phrases should be in the client's own words and describe the present, such as the room, the date and who is near. Stop or shift if the client seems flooded, and be mindful of reporting duties where they apply.

fields.label: Where I am right now
Today's date and what I can see that shows it
One thing that is different now
A person or place that feels steady
A phrase that helps me stay here
What I will do if the phrase does not help

title: Coping Skill Trial Run Sheet
summary: Lets a client test a coping skill in a real moment and review what it did for them.
goal: Match coping skills to the moments and values where they help.
body_md: Have the client pick one skill and one situation, then log what happened without judging it. A skill that fails is useful data, so ask what it gave them and what it cost. Follow with a review in session and decide whether to keep it, adjust it or swap it.

fields.label: The skill I tried
The situation where I used it
What I felt before and after
What the skill helped me do
What it cost me or got in the way of
Whether I will keep, change or swap it

title: Body in Motion Values Walk
summary: A gentle walk or movement practice that links what the body can do to what the client cares about.
goal: Move attention from appearance to function and values.
body_md: Invite the client to walk or move and notice what the body does for them, such as carrying them to people and places they care about. Keep the focus on experience and meaning, never on how the body looks. Stay curious if judgments surface, and let the client set the pace.

fields.label: What my body let me do today
A place or person my body takes me to
A kind word I could say to my body
A judgment that showed up and what I did with it
A valued activity I want to do this week
How I felt after the walk

title: One-Mindfully Single Task Practice
summary: Guides the client through doing one everyday task with full attention and noting each drift.
goal: Build the habit of one thing at a time and gently returning attention.
body_md: Pick a low-stakes task such as washing a cup or folding laundry and run it in session first. Clients tend to judge each drift as failure, so count the returns instead of the drifts. Ask about the pace of the task afterward, since rushing often shows up before the client notices it.

fields.label: The one task I chose to do with full attention
What I noticed in my hands, eyes, and body while doing it
How many times my mind wandered, and where it went
What I said to myself when I noticed, and what I will say next time
One more everyday task I could try this week

title: Turning the Mind Commitment Log
summary: Tracks the moments a client notices resistance and chooses to turn toward acceptance again.
goal: Practice re-committing to acceptance each time resistance returns.
body_md: Explain that turning the mind is a choice made again and again, not a single decision. Review the log for times when resistance showed up with a body cue, since that cue is often the most useful early signal. Keep the tone curious and avoid treating repeated entries as setbacks.

fields.label: The situation where I noticed I was resisting
What resistance felt like in my body
The words I used to turn my mind toward acceptance
What I did next, even if it was small
What got in the way of turning my mind today
What I want to try again tomorrow

title: Describe the Emotion Ladder
summary: Helps a client move from one broad feeling word to more precise words for what is happening.
goal: Name emotions with more precision so they can be understood and handled.
body_md: Many clients start with words like bad or stressed. Work up the ladder slowly and let them reject words that do not fit. Precise naming tends to lower the pressure on its own, so pause to notice any shift before moving on. Keep a short list of their own words for next time.

fields.label: The broad word I started with
Three more specific words that might fit
The words that fit best and where I feel them in my body
What set this feeling off
What the feeling seems to be telling me
How strong it is on a scale of 0 to 10 right now

title: Weekly Skills Review Sheet
summary: Gives client and clinician a short, structured look back at which skills were used and what happened.
goal: Spot which skills helped, which did not, and what to practice next.
body_md: Open the session with this so the review has a steady place. Focus on what the client tried, not on how well it worked, and ask about skills they skipped without judgment. Patterns across weeks are usually more useful than any single day.

fields.label: Skills I used this week
A time a skill helped and what it did
A time I wanted to use a skill but did not
What got in the way
A skill I want to practice more next week
Support I would like from my clinician

title: Safe Place Imagery Card
summary: Builds a calm, personal place in the mind that a client can return to for stabilizing.
goal: Give the client a steady, practiced place to settle when distress rises.
body_md: Build this slowly, in session, with the client in charge of every detail and free to stop at any point. Choose a place that is neutral or pleasant, and never ask about distressing memories. If the image brings up unease, change it or switch to grounding. Practice short and often.

fields.label: Where my safe place is, real or imagined
What I see there
What I hear and smell there
What my body feels like there
A word or phrase that brings me back to it
When I will practice this during the week
What I will do if the image stops feeling safe

title: Low Energy Day Skills Menu
summary: Lists small, doable skills matched to days when energy and motivation are very low.
goal: Keep a few manageable actions available on the hardest days.
body_md: Build the menu together when the client is having a steadier day. Keep every item small enough to finish in a few minutes, such as opening a curtain or drinking water. Clients often set items too large, so trim them together. If low mood is deepening, use your clinical judgment about next steps.

fields.label: Three tiny actions I can do in under five minutes
One skill that helps my body, such as moving or a warm shower
One skill that helps me reach another person
One thing I can let go of for today
Words I can say to myself on a low-energy day
Who I could tell if the day stays heavy
How I will know the menu helped

title: Pause Before Acting Card
summary: Sets up a short, practiced pause between an impulse and the action that follows it.
goal: Create a small gap between impulse and action that the client can use.
body_md: Keep the pause short and concrete so it fits real life, such as three breaths or counting to ten. Rehearse it in session with a recent impulsive moment. Clients with attention difficulties often do better with a visible cue, so plan where the card will live.

fields.label: An impulse that got me into trouble recently
What I notice in my body just before I act
My pause, in plain words, such as three breaths
Where I will keep this card so I see it
What I will do after the pause
Who can remind me to use it
What happened the last time I paused

title: Adaptive Denial Script Card
summary: Helps a client rehearse putting a substance use urge out of mind and moving to another task.
goal: Practice setting an urge aside for now and redirecting attention.
body_md: Explain that this is a short-term skill for moments when an urge is loud, not a way of pretending the urge is absent. Rehearse the script aloud and choose a task that fully occupies the hands. Review with the client what worked and what did not, and keep the language free of labels.

fields.label: A situation where substance use urges are strong
The words I will say to myself to put the urge aside for now
The task I will move to
Who I can contact if the urge stays strong
What I will do if the urge keeps rising
What I will tell myself after the urge passes

title: Thought Observing Practice Log
summary: Trains a client to watch intrusive thoughts come and go without arguing with them or acting on them.
goal: Practice noticing a thought as a thought, without a ritual or reply.
body_md: Explain that the aim is to notice, not to make thoughts stop. Model a light, curious label such as there is that thought again. Clients may turn the practice into a hidden way of seeking certainty, so check how it is going and keep sessions brief.

fields.label: The thought I noticed
What I felt in my body when it showed up
The label I gave it
What I did instead of replying or acting on it
How long it took before my attention moved on
What I want to try next time

title: Sensation Describing Practice
summary: Has a client name body sensations during panic in plain, factual words without judging them.
goal: Describe physical sensations accurately so they feel less alarming.
body_md: Use it when the client reads sensations as danger. Practice in session with a neutral sensation first, then a stronger one. Keep the language factual, such as tight, warm, or fluttering. Note how the description shifts attention, and do not push the client into sensations they are not ready for.

fields.label: The sensation I noticed and where it was
Factual words for it, such as warm or tight
The story my mind added to it
How strong it was from 0 to 10
What I did to let it be there for a minute
What changed as I kept describing it
What I want to practice this week

title: Night Shift Request Script
summary: Helps a new parent ask a partner or helper for specific support with nights and sleep.
goal: Turn an exhausted wish for help into one clear, doable request.
body_md: New parents often hint and hope instead of asking. Have the client write the request in plain words and say it aloud. Keep it concrete, such as one block of protected sleep. Note any feelings of guilt that come up, and use your judgment about further support.

fields.label: What I most need help with at night
Who I am asking
The facts of the situation in one sentence
How I feel about it, using I
My specific request, including when
What I can offer in return
What I will do if the answer is no

title: Proud Moments Mastery Log
summary: Records small actions done well each day so a client can see evidence of capability.
goal: Build a record of competence that counters a harsh self-view.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Ask for small, specific moments rather than big achievements. Clients with a harsh self-view often dismiss entries, so ask what they would say if a friend had done the same thing. Review the log together and read back a few entries aloud.

fields.label: Something I did today that took effort
Why it counts, even if it was small
What strength or skill I used
How I felt in my body when I finished
What a close friend would say about it
One small thing I want to do tomorrow

title: After the Event Facts Review
summary: Helps a client look back on a social event and check the story their mind told about it.
goal: Check the post-event story against what actually happened.
body_md: Use it after a real social situation when the client is replaying it. Have them separate what happened from what they imagined others thought. The review works best when it includes neutral or good moments, which are often left out. Stop the review if it turns into more rumination.

fields.label: What happened, in facts a camera could record
What my mind said about how it went
The facts that fit that story
The facts that do not fit it
A fairer way to describe the event
One thing that went okay
What I will do to let the event go

title: Repair After Conflict Sheet
summary: Plans a calm, sincere repair after an argument, using DBT interpersonal skills.
goal: Move from a painful conflict to a plan for repair that keeps self-respect.
body_md: Work on this once the client has calmed down, not in the middle of distress. Clients often want to explain first; ask what the other person most needs to hear. Keep repair and self-respect both in the plan, and rehearse the opening line aloud.

fields.label: What happened, in facts only
What I am willing to own in the conflict
What I am not willing to give up
What the other person may need to hear
My opening line for the repair
The skill I will use if it gets tense
When and where I will talk

title: Trusted Support Circle Map
summary: Maps who is safe and steady in a client's life and what each person can offer.
goal: Identify and strengthen safe sources of support at the client's own pace.
body_md: Let the client set the pace and leave out any details of what happened. Start with the people and places that feel even a little safe, and respect the decision to keep the circle small. Clients may find it hard to ask for help, so plan one small ask together and review it.

fields.label: People who feel safe to be around
A place that feels calming
What each person can offer, such as listening or company
What I do not want to talk about, and how I can say so
One small request I could make this week
A way to reach someone when I feel unsteady
What helps me feel I have a choice in asking

title: Willingness Ladder for Feared Situations
summary: Builds a stepwise ladder of feared situations with a willing stance toward each small step.
goal: Pair small, chosen steps toward feared things with acceptance skills.
body_md: Have the client rate each step and choose one they are willing to try, not one they think they should. Pair the step with a skill they will use during it. Keep the steps small and review after each one, since repeating a step is fine.

fields.label: The feared situation I want to move toward
Five steps from easiest to hardest
My willingness for each step from 0 to 10
The first step I will try and when
The skill I will use during it
What I expect to feel
What I noticed afterward

title: Body Appreciation Mindfulness Practice
summary: Invites a client to notice what the body does and to meet hard moments with kindness.
goal: Shift attention from looks to function and respond to hard moments with care.
body_md: Keep the focus on what the body does, such as walking, hugging, or breathing, and avoid any talk about size or shape. Clients may find this awkward at first, so offer small, honest steps. Watch for discomfort and let the client skip items that feel forced.

fields.label: Three things my body did for me today
A moment I felt at ease in my body
A critical thought that showed up and what I noticed about it
A kind sentence I could say to myself in that moment
One caring thing I can do for my body today
Who I can talk with when the thoughts get loud

title: Weekend Reconnection Planner
summary: Two partners each plan one small shared activity and one solo recharge for the weekend.
goal: Build a predictable pocket of connection without either partner feeling crowded.
body_md: Have each partner fill in their own side first, then compare. Couples often plan too much, so cap it at one shared activity. Notice whether one partner's recharge time reads as rejection to the other, and name that out loud before the weekend.

fields.label: Partner A: one thing I would enjoy doing together this weekend
Partner B: one thing I would enjoy doing together this weekend
Partner A: how I like to recharge on my own
Partner B: how I like to recharge on my own
Together: the one shared activity we chose and when
Together: how we will say so kindly if we need a change of plan

title: Two Sides of One Story Retelling
summary: Each partner retells a recent disagreement from the other partner's point of view.
goal: Build perspective-taking before problem-solving begins.
body_md: Choose a low-intensity disagreement, not the biggest one. Partner A retells it as Partner B experienced it, then Partner B corrects gently and adds what was missed. Stop the exercise if either partner becomes flooded. The point is being understood, not agreeing on the facts.

fields.label: Partner A: the disagreement in one sentence
Partner A: how I think Partner B felt during it
Partner B: what Partner A got right about my side
Partner B: what Partner A missed about my side
Partner B: the disagreement in one sentence
Partner B: how I think Partner A felt during it
Partner A: what Partner B got right about my side
Together: one thing we each understand better now

title: Shared Calendar Expectations Talk
summary: Partners compare how each expects time, plans and commitments to be handled.
goal: Surface mismatched expectations about time before they turn into resentment.
body_md: Mismatched expectations about plans, lateness and last-minute changes often sit under recurring arguments. Ask each partner to write before speaking. Watch for one partner treating their own style as the standard, and help them frame differences as preferences rather than flaws.

fields.label: Partner A: how I like plans to be made and shared
Partner B: how I like plans to be made and shared
Partner A: what being late or changing plans means to me
Partner B: what being late or changing plans means to me
Together: one calendar habit we will try for two weeks
Together: how we will check whether it is working

title: Gratitude Letters Swap for Couples
summary: Partners write short notes naming specific things they value and read them aloud.
goal: Give each partner specific, spoken appreciation they can keep.
body_md: Ask for specifics, not general praise: an actual moment and what it showed about the partner. Some people deflect compliments, so coach the listener to simply say thank you. Listening without rebuttal is part of the exercise, and worth debriefing afterward.

fields.label: Partner A: a moment this month when I felt grateful for you
Partner A: what that moment showed me about you
Partner B: a moment this month when I felt grateful for you
Partner B: what that moment showed me about you
Partner A: how it felt to hear Partner B's note
Partner B: how it felt to hear Partner A's note

title: Decision-Making Style Comparison
summary: Partners map how each prefers to make joint decisions and where the styles collide.
goal: Reduce standoffs by making each partner's decision style visible.
body_md: Some people decide fast and revisit, others research before committing, and each can read the other as careless or stalling. Use a recent decision as the example. Help the couple agree on a shared process, such as a deadline plus one veto each, rather than picking a winner.

fields.label: Partner A: how I usually like to make a big decision
Partner B: how I usually like to make a big decision
Partner A: what I find hard about Partner B's style
Partner B: what I find hard about Partner A's style
Together: a recent decision where our styles collided
Together: a process for our next decision that respects both styles

title: Trauma Triggers and Partner Grounding Card
summary: Partners record one person's known reminders and the grounding help the other can offer.
goal: Give the supporting partner a clear, agreed way to help during a hard moment.
body_md: Keep this about present-day cues and support, never about retelling what happened. Let the partner who has the reminders lead and set the pace. The supporting partner's job is to offer agreed grounding, not to question. Revisit the card regularly since what helps can change.

fields.label: Partner A: a few reminders that can make things feel unsafe for me now
Partner A: signs in my body that I am getting overwhelmed
Partner A: what helps me feel grounded and what does not
Partner B: what I will say and do when I notice those signs
Partner B: what I will avoid doing
Together: the signal Partner A can give to ask for space or help
Together: who else we can turn to for support

title: Low Energy Day Partner Menu
summary: A menu where the partner with low mood picks the help they want and the other offers it.
goal: Replace guessing and pressure with a simple menu of support on hard days.
body_md: Pressure to cheer up and helpful fixing both tend to backfire on low days. A menu lets the partner with low mood choose without explaining. Coach the other partner to offer the item without debating it. Review together what worked, and adjust the menu as needs change.

title: Shared Systems Design Session
summary: Partners design one shared routine together, with each person's strengths named up front.
goal: Build a household system around how both partners' attention really works.
body_md: Start with strengths, not failures, so the partner with attention difficulties is not cast as the problem. Choose one routine only, such as mornings or bills. Systems that live in view, like a whiteboard or shared alarm, tend to outlast reminders spoken by one partner to the other.

title: Anger Repair Conversation Planner
summary: Partners plan the conversation they will have after an angry moment has passed.
goal: Turn cooled-down anger into repair rather than silence or blame.
body_md: Use this only once both partners are calm, and stop if anyone escalates. The partner who got angry goes first, naming their part without a but. Then the other shares the impact. Check that the repair includes one concrete change, not just an apology.

title: Reassurance Pause Agreement for Partners
summary: Partners agree on a gentler response than repeated reassurance when intrusive worries spike.
goal: Replace repeated reassuring with a plan both partners can live with.
body_md: Repeated reassurance can ease things briefly and keep worries going. Build the agreement together and avoid framing it as withdrawal of love. The supporting partner needs a warm line to say instead. Go slowly, and expect both partners to feel uncomfortable at first.

title: Panic Night Plan for Couples
summary: Partners write a simple plan for a panic episode that strikes at night.
goal: Give both partners a script for the night so neither has to improvise.
body_md: Night episodes leave the partner frightened and unsure. Write the plan when both are calm. Keep it short enough to follow half asleep. Ask the partner with panic what they want said, and the other partner what they need so they can stay steady. Rehearse it once in session.

title: Postpartum Couple Reconnection Plan
summary: New parents each name what they miss and plan one small moment of connection.
goal: Protect a few minutes of couple connection while the household is stretched thin.
body_md: New parents are often tired and invisible to each other. Keep the plan very small, such as ten minutes after the baby sleeps. Let each partner say what they miss without it becoming a complaint. Encourage them to talk with their clinician or doctor if low mood or worry seems to be growing.

summary: Each partner shares one harsh self-judgment and hears how the other sees them.
goal: Let partners offer each other a kinder, more accurate view than the inner critic's.
body_md: Ask the speaker to name the critic's words in the third person to soften the pull. The listener reflects what they see in their partner, without arguing or flooding with praise. Watch for compliments that are rejected, and invite the speaker to simply notice how it lands.

title: Grief Anniversaries Plan for Couples
summary: Partners plan how to spend a hard date, with each person's wishes named.
goal: Prepare for a painful date so neither partner is surprised by the other's needs.
body_md: Partners can grieve differently, one wanting company and the other quiet. Plan ahead for a birthday, anniversary or holiday. Make space for both needs, and build in a fallback if the day goes differently. Leave room for unplanned feelings and for asking others to share the day.

title: Weekly Relationship Rating Review
summary: Partners privately rate several areas of the relationship, then compare and choose one focus.
goal: Give both partners a simple shared picture of what is working and what needs attention.
body_md: Rate privately before sharing to avoid anchoring on the first partner's answers. Differences in ratings are useful information, not a contest. Help the couple choose one area only for the coming week and agree on one small action each.

title: Paced Closeness Conversation Guide
summary: Partners talk about touch, closeness and pacing, with one partner's choices leading.
goal: Support a survivor's sense of choice and safety while keeping partners connected.
body_md: Use only with the survivor's consent and pacing, and never ask for details of the past. The survivor sets the agenda, including yes, no and later. The other partner practices hearing no without hurt or pressure. Consider whether individual support alongside the couple work would help.

title: Fear Facing Teamwork Plan
summary: Partners agree how the supporter can cheer on each small step a partner takes toward a fear.
goal: Keep the supporting partner encouraging without pushing, rescuing or avoiding.
body_md: Support can slide into rescuing or rushing. Agree on the supporter's role before a practice begins. The partner facing the fear chooses the step and the pace. Ask the supporter to notice effort, not outcome, and plan how they both respond if the step is stopped early.

title: Self-Talk and Partner Words Exchange
summary: Partners share how they talk about their own appearance and agree on supportive language.
goal: Help couples build language that supports each person's feelings about their body.
body_md: Focus on words and feelings, never on any measurement or rule. Ask each partner how they speak about themselves in front of the other, and how the other's words land. Agree on phrases that feel kind and on topics each partner prefers to leave alone.

title: Mood Garden Drawing
summary: The child draws a garden where each plant stands for a feeling and the weather around it.
goal: Give a child a picture language for moods they cannot yet name aloud.
body_md: Hand over paper and crayons and let the child pick which feelings get a plant, then ask what each one needs to grow or rest. Keep your questions curious and let the drawing lead. Invite the parent for the last five minutes to hear the garden tour and to water one plant at home with a kind word this week.

title: Pillow Fort Calm Corner Build
summary: The child and parent build a small cozy corner at home and stock it with calming items.
goal: Create a reliable physical spot where a child can settle before a big feeling grows.
body_md: Build a mini version in the office with cushions and a blanket, then plan the home version together. The parent's job is to stay nearby and never use the corner as a punishment. Watch for a child who wants it only as a hiding place and talk through when it helps and when a grown-up check-in helps more.

title: Friendship Recipe Card Game
summary: Players draw ingredient cards and build a silly recipe for being a good friend.
goal: Practice the small moves of friendship through play and a shared debrief.
body_md: Each player takes a turn drawing a card such as sharing, listening or saying sorry, acting it out, and adding it to the recipe bowl. The group votes on which ingredient was hardest to do. Debrief on one ingredient each child will try this week. Keep the tone light so a shy child can pass once without losing face.

title: Bedtime Worry Letterbox
summary: The child decorates a box and posts worries on paper before bed so the night can be quiet.
goal: Give a child a simple ritual to hand worries off before sleep.
body_md: Decorate a shoebox as a letterbox together and practice drawing or dictating a worry and posting it. The parent reads nothing at night and opens the box at a set morning time with the child. Explain that the box holds worries without solving them. If a child names fear for their safety, follow your usual duty to report and share the concern with the caregiver.

goal: Help a child notice and collect moments of kindness in daily life.
body_md: Cut paper strips and start the first link in session, then send the chain home. The parent writes or draws what the child reports on each link without adding commentary or rewards. Review the chain the next visit and ask which link felt best to make. Children who find it hard to think of a link can use kindness they received.

title: Worry Weather Forecast Board
summary: The child draws a forecast for the day's worries and plans a small umbrella for each.
goal: Help a child predict, name and plan for worry instead of being caught off guard.
body_md: Use a large sheet as a weather map and let the child place sun, cloud and storm symbols for situations ahead. Pair each cloud with one small coping choice. The parent learns to ask about the forecast at breakfast instead of reassuring repeatedly. If reassurance seeking comes up, plan together how the parent can respond warmly and briefly.

summary: The child maps a day into gray cloud and sunshine moments with stickers and drawing.
goal: Let a child show how low mood moves through a day and where small lifts exist.
body_md: Draw a simple day line and place stickers for gray cloud and sunny times. Be curious about the sunny ones, however small, and wonder aloud what was different. The parent adds one planned sunny moment to the week and joins in without expecting cheerfulness. If a child talks about not wanting to be here, stay with them and ask about 988 (call or text) with the caregiver in session.

summary: A drawn race track turns the morning or homework routine into laps with stopping points.
goal: Break a hard routine into visible steps so a child with busy attention can follow along.
body_md: Draw a track with a start, four to six pit stops and a finish, and let the child name each stop and decorate their car. Keep the steps short and the parent's job to point at the track rather than repeat instructions. Try it for one routine only and review what got stuck. Adjust stops together rather than adding more.

summary: The child draws a three-panel comic of a blowup, a pause and a better ending.
goal: Help a child rehearse a pause between a mad feeling and what they do with it.
body_md: Let the child draw a recent frustrating moment in panel one, the pause in panel two and the new ending in panel three, with stick figures welcomed. Praise the pause, not the drawing. The parent reads the comic with the child and agrees on one cue word for the pause. Practice the pause in session with a calm voice model from you.

goal: Help a child see intrusive doubts as a pushy voice they can talk back to.
body_md: Ask the child to draw the doubting voice as a silly character and give it a name, then fill a speech bubble with what it says and another with a bold comeback. The parent learns to say something like that sounds like the doubter instead of answering the question. Watch for rituals hiding inside the comic and keep the focus on not obeying the voice.

goal: Give parents a steady weekly rhythm for connection and small shared decisions.
body_md: Invite the parent and child to decorate a team board together and choose a short weekly huddle time. The parent speaks first about something they noticed going well, then the child. Keep problems for later in the huddle and keep the huddle under ten minutes. Notice who talks most and gently even the turns out.

body_md: Fold paper into a little book and draw pages such as what is changing, what stays the same and what the baby cannot do yet. The parent joins to add one thing they love about the child and one special moment just for them. Listen for a parent who sounds exhausted or low and follow up with them privately and gently.

goal: Build a child's sense of worth through specific, honest strengths.
body_md: Cut medals from cardboard and let the child name each one for something real, like helping a friend or trying again. Avoid inflated praise and ask how they know it is true. The parent adds one medal of their own for the child and hangs the set at home. If the child struggles, offer a medal for effort or kindness.

goal: Give a grieving child a gentle way to say what they want to say to someone they lost.
body_md: Offer paper, markers and a balloon outline, and let the child lead what goes in the message. Sit close and let silence be fine. The parent chooses a safe moment at home to let the balloon go or keep it and is told that grief arrives in waves. Go at the child's pace and stop if the feeling is too big.

body_md: Draw a river with two banks and let the child and a parent take turns adding planks that say a feeling and a need. Each person listens without fixing. The debrief asks what it was like to hear the other person. Keep turns equal and keep the bridge simple so a child who is worried about conflict stays comfortable.

body_md: Cut a paper wheel with six slices and let the child fill each with a drawn choice, like squeeze a pillow or draw scribbles. Spin and practice the tool right away. The parent can spin with the child during hard moments instead of offering advice. Retire tools that are not working rather than adding pressure.

goal: Plan small, repeatable steps toward a fear the child wants to face.

The parent practices staying calm and not rescuing, and cheers the effort rather than the lack of fear. Stop climbing if the step is too big and shrink it.

title: Partner Puzzle Pieces Game
