The point is that discomfort can come along while they move toward what they care about. Avoid framing it as getting rid of nerves, and ask them to choose one action that fits a value, not a performance goal.

fields.label: The kind of person I want to be around others
A relationship I want to grow
What anxiety says when I move toward it
What I do instead when anxiety is loud
A small action that fits my value
The discomfort I am willing to carry
When I will take the step
What I noticed afterward

title: Calm Body Before People Card
summary: A DBT skills card for settling the body before and during a social event.
goal: Use distress tolerance skills to steady a racing body in social moments.
body_md: Practice the skills in session before your client tries them in the wild, since new skills rarely work first try under pressure. Offer a few options such as paced breathing, cold water on the hands, and a grounding look around the room, and let them choose. Ask them to rate their body before and after to see what helps.

fields.label: A social situation that makes my body react
Signs in my body I notice first
Distress level before (0 to 10)
The skill I chose from the list
What I did, step by step
Distress level after (0 to 10)
What I would change next time
Where I will keep this card

title: Anniversary Plan for Two
summary: A shared plan for a hard date, with each partner naming what they need and what they can offer.
goal: Help two grieving partners plan a difficult date without leaving either one alone with it.
body_md: Partners often grieve a shared loss on different timelines and guess at what the other wants on a hard date. Have each partner fill in their own side first, then compare. Notice where one wants company and the other wants space, and help them build a plan that holds both. Revisit it after the date.

fields.label: Date or season we are planning for
Partner A: what I hope this day looks like
Partner B: what I hope this day looks like
Partner A: one thing I need from you that day
Partner B: one thing I need from you that day
Something we will do together
Something each of us may do alone, and how we will check in
How we will know if one of us needs to change the plan

title: Our Family Remembering Tree
summary: A drawn tree where a child adds leaves for memories, feelings and questions about someone who died.
goal: Give a grieving child a drawn, hands-on way to hold memories and questions alongside a caregiver.
body_md: Give the child paper and colored pencils and draw a bare tree together. Each leaf holds a memory, a feeling or a question, and the child decides what goes on it. The parent sits alongside, listens, and adds a leaf of their own without correcting anything. If a child discloses harm or abuse while drawing, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw the tree and write the name of the person we are remembering
Draw three leaves for happy memories
Draw a leaf for a hard feeling and give it a color
Draw a leaf for a question I still have
Parent: a leaf with one memory of your own to share
Where we will keep the tree and when we will add more leaves

title: Memory Lane Turns Game
summary: A turn-taking card game where players share stories and feelings about someone who died.
goal: Make it easier for family members to talk about a loss by taking small, chosen turns.
body_md: Players take turns drawing a prompt card and may share, pass, or swap with the next player; passing is always allowed. Write the cards together with the group in advance, mixing light memories with harder ones. Keep the pace slow and close with a debrief on what it was like to hear each other. Watch for the quiet player who passes every turn.

fields.label: Rules we all agree on before we start
Prompt cards I want to add: a favorite memory
Prompt cards I want to add: something I miss
Prompt cards I want to add: something I wish I could say
One thing I heard from someone else that stayed with me
How my body felt during the game
What I want to do differently with these stories after today

title: Loss Ripple Effects Sheet
summary: A page for tracing how a loss touches routines, roles, relationships and plans beyond the sadness.
goal: Show a client the secondary changes a loss brings so they can name what else needs attention.
body_md: Grief is often reduced to sadness, yet clients describe losing roles, routines and a future they had pictured. Use the sheet to make those ripples visible so you can sort them into what needs grieving, what needs practical help, and what can wait. Expect some clients to find one area much heavier than the rest.

fields.label: The loss, in a sentence
Daily routines that changed
Roles I held that are different now
Relationships that shifted
Plans or hopes for the future that changed
Practical tasks that piled up
Which ripple weighs most right now
Who could help with one of these this week

title: What Grief Tells Me Record
summary: A thought record for grief that separates painful but accurate thoughts from ones that add extra weight.
goal: Help a client tell apart the thoughts that fit the loss from the ones that deepen distress.
body_md: Unlike a standard thought record, this one does not try to talk anyone out of sadness. Clients mark which thoughts are true and painful, and look more closely at the ones phrased as absolutes, such as never or always. Go gently, as some thoughts that look like traps are part of honoring the person. Let the client choose which to keep.

fields.label: The moment grief hit hard
The thought that came with it
Feeling and how strong it was, 0 to 100
Is this thought true and painful, or does it add extra weight
Evidence that fits the thought
Words like always or never in the thought
A kinder version that still honors the loss
How I feel after rewriting it

title: Relationship Values Gap Sheet
summary: Compares the partner a client wants to be with what they actually did this week, without blame.
goal: Help a client notice the gap between valued relationship actions and recent choices, then pick one step.
body_md: This is a values-and-committed-action tool for a client working on their own side of a relationship. Keep the focus on chosen actions, not on the partner's behavior. Expect some clients to turn the gap into a verdict on themselves, so go back to what they care about. Pick one small action they can take this week.

fields.label: The kind of partner I want to be
A moment this week that matched it
A moment this week that did not match
What got in the way: thoughts, feelings, urges
A willing stance toward those feelings
One small action I will take this week
How I will notice I did it

title: Interpersonal Effectiveness Plan
summary: Plans a hard conversation using DEAR MAN, GIVE and FAST steps, with a rehearsal line for each.
goal: Help a client prepare a specific request or boundary with a partner using interpersonal skills.
body_md: Choose one real conversation the client wants to have. Work through DEAR MAN for the request, then GIVE for keeping the relationship intact and FAST for self-respect, and rehearse the opening lines aloud in session. Clients often skip the Mindful step and drift to other topics, so practice repeating the ask calmly.

fields.label: The situation and who it is with
Describe: the facts only
Express: how I feel about it
Assert: what I am asking for
Reinforce: what is good for both of us
Gentle, interested, easy: how I will keep the tone
Fair and truthful: what I will not say or do
Rehearsal: my first two sentences

title: Daily Appreciation and Ask Sheet
summary: A short shared sheet where each partner offers one appreciation and one small ask each day.
goal: Build a daily habit of noticing the good and making clear, small requests between two partners.
duration: Five minutes daily for two weeks
body_md: Each partner completes their own side once a day and shares it at a set time. Appreciations must be specific, and asks must be small, positive and doable that day. Watch for asks that are criticisms in disguise. Review the pattern together at the next session, and note what each partner learned from the other's answers.

fields.label: Partner A: something I appreciated about you today
Partner A: one small thing I would like tomorrow
Partner B: something I appreciated about you today
Partner B: one small thing I would like tomorrow
What I did with the other's ask
What was hard about doing this
What we will keep

title: Home of Our Family Drawing
summary: A drawing activity where a child shows who lives in the family home and how each person feels.
goal: Let a child show how they see the relationships at home without needing the words for it.
body_md: Ask the child to draw the house, put each family member in a room, and add a color for each person's feelings. The parent watches and listens without correcting the picture, and later can add a room of their own. Treat the drawing as the child's view, not a fact. If a child discloses harm, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: Draw your house and the people in it
Pick a color for how each person feels most days
Draw where you like to be most
Draw one thing you wish was different at home
Draw something that helps when people are upset
Parent: one thing you heard from the drawing

title: Fair Fight Referee Game
summary: A role-play game where partners practice a disagreement while a referee flags rule breaks.
goal: Give couples a low-stakes way to practice fair argument rules and notice their own habits.
body_md: Set rules together: no name-calling, one person talks at a time, a time-out is always allowed. Partners argue a mild, made-up topic while a referee, you or a second pair, flags rule breaks with a card. Swap roles each round, then debrief on what each person noticed. Keep it light and stop the game if a real conflict surfaces.

fields.label: Our agreed rules for a fair fight
The mild topic we picked
A rule I broke
A rule my partner kept well
What the referee noticed
What I felt in my body when I was flagged
One rule I want us to use at home

title: Window of Comfort Map
summary: A page for mapping what feels settled, too activated or too numb, with grounding steps for each.
goal: Help a client recognize their own states and choose a stabilizing step without revisiting what happened.
body_md: This stays in the present: clients map how their body and mind feel when settled, wound up or shut down, and which steps help. Never ask for details of what happened. Let the client choose the pace and skip any box. Practice one grounding step in session so it is familiar before they need it at home.

fields.label: What feeling settled is like for me
Signs I am getting wound up
Signs I am shutting down
Something that helps when I am wound up
Something that helps when I am shut down
A person or place that feels safe
The step I will try this week

title: Safe Present Thought Check
summary: A thought record for here-and-now moments when old fear shows up in a safe setting.
goal: Help a client check the present moment against a fear that arrives unannounced.
body_md: This record covers only the present moment: where the client is, who is there, and what is different now. It never asks about the past event. Look for thoughts that treat the present as the past, and let the client lead on which ones to examine. Stop and ground first if a memory begins to take over.

fields.label: Where I am right now
What set off the feeling
The thought that came with it
How strong the feeling was, 0 to 100
What I can see, hear and touch around me
What is different about now
A thought that fits the present
How strong the feeling is now

title: Self-Kindness Pause Practice
summary: A short pause for responding to harsh self-talk with kindness, with room to notice and let thoughts pass.
goal: Help a client meet shame-filled self-talk with distance and kindness, and then take a small caring action.
body_md: Clients may carry harsh thoughts about themselves that are not about what happened but about who they are. Introduce a pause: notice the thought, name it as a thought, and offer yourself what you would offer a friend. Choose a gentle phrase together in session. Do not push; the client decides how close to get.

fields.label: A harsh thought I had about myself
Notice it: I am having the thought that...
What I would say to a friend who thought this
A kind phrase I can use
Where I feel the kindness in my body
A small caring action I can do today
Who I can share this practice with

title: Self-Soothe Kit Builder
summary: Builds a personal kit of soothing options for each of the five senses to use when feeling overwhelmed.
goal: Help a client assemble ready-to-use sensory soothing options for hard moments.
body_md: Work through each sense and have the client test options in session: a scent, a texture, a sound, a taste, something to look at. Choose items that are safe and truly soothing for them, not what they think they should like. Some sensory items can be unexpected triggers, so let them drop any that are. Check in on what they actually try.

fields.label: Something I can look at that calms me
A sound that settles me
A scent I find comforting
A taste I enjoy
A texture or touch that feels safe
Where I will keep my kit
When I will try it this week
What I noticed when I tried it

title: Partner Pacing Agreement for Support
summary: A partner-pacing tool where one partner sets the pace of closeness and the other offers steady support.
goal: Help partners agree on a pace, a stop signal and a way to reconnect, without discussing what happened.
body_md: This is about pacing and safety in the present. The partner who is a survivor decides what feels comfortable, and the supportive partner commits to following that pace. Neither partner shares details of what happened. Agree on a stop signal and a way to reconnect afterward, and revisit the agreement as things change.

fields.label: Survivor partner: things that help me feel safe near you
Survivor partner: our stop signal
Supportive partner: how I will follow your pace
Supportive partner: how I will respond when you use the signal
How we will reconnect after a pause
What we will do when we disagree about the pace
When we will review this agreement

title: Coping Skills Superhero Cape
summary: A child decorates a paper cape with the skills that help them when feelings get big.
goal: Help a child name and remember a few coping skills in a playful, wearable form.
body_md: Give the child a paper or felt cape shape and markers, and let them pick a hero name. Each skill earns a cape symbol: a drawn balloon for slow breaths, a heart for asking for a hug. Keep it to three or four skills. Invite the parent for the last ten minutes so the child can teach them, and tell the parent to remind, not command, when feelings rise. If a child discloses harm or abuse while drawing, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: My hero name
Skill one and the symbol I drew for it
Skill two and the symbol I drew for it
Skill three and the symbol I drew for it
When my cape helps me most
What my grown-up can say to remind me

title: Coping Skills Weather Report
summary: A turn-taking game where players forecast a feeling and pick a skill to match the weather.
goal: Practice matching a coping skill to the intensity of a feeling in a low-pressure group game.
body_md: Players sit in a circle with a deck of skill cards and a pile of weather cards (drizzle, thunderstorm, fog, heat wave). On a turn, draw a weather card, say what kind of moment it stands for, and choose a skill card from the table that fits; the group votes thumbs up or down, and one point goes to a good match. Play ten minutes, then debrief on which skills fit which weather. Let passing be allowed so nobody is cornered.

fields.label: The weather card I drew and the moment it stood for
The skill I chose and why it fit
A skill the group picked that I would not have thought of
A weather type where I still lack a good skill
One skill I will try this week and when

title: First Ten Minutes Plan
summary: A short plan for what to do in the first ten minutes after a hard moment begins.
goal: Give a client a pre-decided sequence of small steps for the early minutes of distress.
body_md: The first minutes often decide whether a hard moment grows, so build the plan when the client is calm. Ask for steps small enough to do while upset: moving rooms, cold water, one text to a person. Rehearse the first step aloud in session. Clients tend to write ambitious plans, so trim anything that needs equipment or a good mood. Review after a week and swap out whatever they skipped.

fields.label: A moment that tends to start a rough stretch
The first sign that it is starting
Minute one to two: what I do
Minute three to five: what I do
Minute six to ten: what I do
Who I can contact if the ten minutes are not enough
What I will check on after the ten minutes pass

title: Coping Thought Swap Cards
summary: A thought record variation where an unhelpful thought is swapped for a more balanced one.
goal: Help a client notice an unhelpful thought and build a balanced alternative they can reach for.
body_md: Use this after the client knows what a thinking trap is. They copy a thought from a hard moment onto one side of a card, then work out evidence for and against it, and write a balanced version on the other side. The card is meant to fit in a pocket. Watch for swaps that are forced positivity; the balanced thought should feel believable at a four or five out of ten, not perfect. Stack the cards over weeks.

fields.label: The situation
The thought that came up
How strongly I believed it, 0 to 10
Evidence that supports it
Evidence that does not fully fit it
A more balanced version I can believe
How I feel after reading the balanced version

title: Making Room While Coping
summary: Separates skills that make room for a feeling from skills that push it away.
goal: Help a client choose coping steps that move them toward what matters while the feeling stays present.
body_md: Ask the client to recall a recent hard moment and list what they did. Then sort each action by whether it made room for the feeling and let them act on a value, or pushed the feeling away. Neither side is bad; the point is to see the pattern. Expect some clients to hear this as being told to just feel it. Name that making room is a choice with a purpose, and plan one small, values-linked action with the feeling coming along.

fields.label: A hard moment and the feeling in it
What I did, listed in order
Which actions pushed the feeling away
Which actions made room for it
What mattered to me in that moment
One small step I could take with the feeling still there
How I will know I made room

title: Calm Scale Distress Card
summary: A card for rating distress and choosing a distress tolerance skill while facing a feared thing.
goal: Pair each step toward a feared thing with a skill that helps the client stay with the distress.
body_md: Fill this in before an approach step, then use it during and after. The client picks one or two skills from the distress tolerance set, such as paced breathing, temperature change or a grounding scan, and rates distress before, during and after. Many clients forget to rate the after number, which is where they see it settle. Practice the skill in the office first so they are not meeting it for the first time at the peak.

fields.label: The step I plan to take toward the feared thing
My distress before, 0 to 10
The skill I will use to stay with it
My distress at the highest point
What I told myself to keep going
My distress after, 0 to 10
What I noticed about how the number moved

title: Coach and Step Back Plan
summary: Both partners agree when to coach and when to step back during one partner's brave steps.
goal: Clarify what the supporting partner does and does not do while the other faces a feared thing.
body_md: Have both partners fill in their own half before comparing. The partner facing the fear says what helps and what pulls them back; the supporting partner names the urge to rescue or push and what they will do instead. Agree on a signal for a pause. Couples often drift into reassuring or taking over, so ask each to describe the other's part in their own words, and set a check-in time after each step to talk about how it went.

fields.label: Partner facing the fear: the step I am taking
Partner facing the fear: what helps me most from you
Partner facing the fear: what does not help
Supporting partner: how I will coach during the step
Supporting partner: what I will not do, such as rescuing or hurrying
Our pause signal and what we do when we use it
When we will check in and what each of us will say

title: Brave Explorer Treasure Map
summary: A child draws a treasure map where each landmark is a small step toward a feared thing.
goal: Help a child see approaching a fear as an adventure made of small, doable steps.
body_md: Let the child draw an island with a start flag and a treasure at the far end, then add three to five landmarks that are steps toward the feared thing, easy ones first. They choose a stamp or sticker for each landmark reached. Tell the parent to praise the trying, stay calm, and avoid pushing past the step the child picked. Do not use the map to force a step. If a child discloses anything worrying while drawing, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: What the treasure at the end of the map is
Landmark one, the easiest step
Landmark two
Landmark three
Landmark four, the hardest step
How my grown-up helps on the trip
The stamp I will give myself for each step

title: Fear Forecast Dice Game
summary: A dice game where players guess how a feared situation will go, then compare with what happened.
goal: Practice noticing the gap between feared predictions and real outcomes in a playful, shared setting.
body_md: Each player names a mild, not a top-rated, situation they have tried or could try. Before acting or recalling the outcome, they roll a die to set their predicted scariness from one to six, then share what really happened and roll again for actual scariness. Compare the two numbers; a gap earns a point for the whole group. Debrief on which predictions ran high. Keep everyone choosing their own situations, and never dare a player to go further.

fields.label: The situation I picked
My predicted scariness number
What I expected to happen
What actually happened
My actual scariness number
What the gap taught me
One situation I could try before our next meeting

title: Fear Avoidance Give and Take Ledger
summary: A ledger of what avoiding a feared thing costs across days, activities and relationships.
goal: Help a client see what the avoidance protects and what it takes away, to inform their own choice.
body_md: The client lists what avoidance gives them (relief, safety) and what it costs (places not visited, plans declined, energy spent planning around it). Go slowly with the cost side; some clients feel blamed. The aim is not to push but to show what is at stake so they decide what to work on. Revisit the ledger every few weeks as steps are taken, and have the client add anything that comes back into their life.

fields.label: The thing I avoid
Ways I avoid it or work around it
What avoiding gives me in the moment
Places, plans or people I miss because of it
Time and energy I spend managing it
Something I would do again if the fear were smaller
The smallest step I would be willing to test

title: Appearance Thought Reframe
summary: A thought record for judgments about how the client looks, ending in a more balanced view.
goal: Help a client catch harsh appearance thoughts and test them against what else is true.
body_md: Start with a recent moment when an appearance thought hit hard. Name the thinking trap (mind reading, all-or-nothing, fortune telling) and then ask what a friend would say about the same thought. Clients often skip the evidence column and write a positive slogan, so hold them to what is actually observable. Do not ask for any measurements or comparisons of the body. Treat the balanced thought as one to try on, not a rule.

fields.label: The moment and where I was
The appearance thought that came up
The feeling and how strong it was, 0 to 10
The thinking trap it fits
What I would say to a friend with this thought
A more balanced thought
How strong the feeling is now

title: Values Over Appearance Compass
summary: A compass that points the client from appearance worries toward actions that matter to them.
goal: Redirect time spent on appearance worries toward valued actions with people and activities.
body_md: Ask the client what appearance worries have kept them from doing, then what they would do if those worries were along for the ride. Have them name two values and a small action for each. Expect clients to want the worry gone first; gently note that the compass works with the worry present. Check back next session on whether the action happened and what the worry did while it did.

fields.label: A moment when appearance worries took over
What those worries kept me from doing
Something I value, such as friendship or play
A small action for that value this week
A second value
A small action for that second value
What I will say to the worry when it comes along

title: Comparison Wave Skill Card
summary: A DBT skills card for riding out the pull of comparison after seeing other people online or in person.
goal: Give a client a step-by-step skill for the surge of feeling after comparing their appearance to others.
body_md: Walk the client through naming the emotion, noticing where it sits, and using opposite action or self-soothing in the moments after comparing. Many clients want to avoid every trigger, so help them choose skills that work even when avoidance fails. Practice the first two steps in session using a mild recalled example. Ask them to bring back the card with one use marked, whether or not it helped.

fields.label: What I saw or heard that started the comparison
The emotion I named
Where I feel it in my body
The urge it brought, such as scrolling or hiding
The opposite action I could take
A self-soothing step I will use
How the feeling changed after the skill

title: Partner Compliment and Comfort Guide
summary: Each partner says which words about appearance land well and which do not.
goal: Help both partners learn what kinds of comments feel supportive when body image worries are present.
body_md: Each partner completes the sheet separately, then they read their answers aloud while the other listens without fixing. The partner with body image worries says what helps and what stings; the other describes what they notice and wish they could say. Couples often default to reassurance that does not land, so look for comments about what the person does or who they are. Close by agreeing on one phrase each to try.

fields.label: Partner with worries: comments that feel warm to me
Partner with worries: comments that do not help, even if kindly meant
Partner with worries: what I wish you would ask me
Supporting partner: what I want to say but hold back
Supporting partner: a comment about who you are that I could offer
What we both will try this week
How we will tell each other if a comment misses

title: My Body Adventure Drawing
summary: A child draws the adventures their body takes them on and what each part helps them do.
goal: Help a child connect their body to play and adventure rather than to how it looks.
body_md: Give the child a big sheet and ask where their body went this week: running, hugging, dancing, climbing. They draw a picture of one adventure and label what their body helped with. Keep the talk on what the body does and enjoys. Tell the parent to notice and name what the child's body does and to avoid comments about looks for the week. If a child discloses harm or abuse, follow your reporting duties.

fields.label: An adventure my body took me on
What my legs, hands or arms helped me do
A thing my body does that I am proud of
Something I like to do with my friends or family
A kind thing I can say about my body
What my grown-up will say when we talk about bodies

title: Double Standard Technique
summary: A sheet where a client writes what they would say to a friend in the same spot, then compares it with their self-talk.
goal: Use it to loosen harsh self-judgments by contrasting them with how the client treats others.
body_md: Pick a recent self-critical thought the client can name easily. Have them write the friend's version first, in the voice they would really use, then set the two side by side. Clients sometimes say a friend is different, so ask what makes that so and whether the rule holds up. Let the comparison do the work and avoid arguing the point for them.

fields.label: The situation and the harsh thing I said to myself.
If a close friend were in this exact situation, I would say this to them.
How my words to myself differ from my words to my friend.
Why I might hold myself to a different rule.
A fairer sentence I could say to myself next time.

title: Naming the Story Practice
summary: A short defusion practice for giving a familiar, repeating mind story a title and noticing it arrive.
goal: Help the client recognize a recurring story as a story, not a fact to obey.
body_md: Have the client pick one story their mind tells again and again, then give it a title, such as The Not Good Enough Story, and notice it when it shows up. The aim is to hold the story more lightly, not to argue with it or prove it wrong. Check whether the title feels playful or dismissive, and adjust the tone with the client so it never turns into mockery of their pain.

fields.label: The story my mind tells again and again
A title I would give that story
Where and when this story tends to show up
What I notice when I say, there is the story, instead of arguing with it
What I would do if I did not have to follow this story today

title: IMPROVE the Moment Card
summary: Walks a client through the IMPROVE the Moment distress tolerance skills for one hard stretch of time.
goal: Give the client a menu of ways to get through a painful moment without making it worse.
body_md: Have the client pick a recent painful moment and try the letters one at a time: imagery, meaning, prayer or connection to something larger, relaxation, one thing in the moment, a vacation of a few minutes, and encouragement. Most clients latch onto one or two letters, so help them choose those and rehearse them in session before they need them.

fields.label: A painful moment I expect this week
Imagery: a calming scene I could picture
Meaning: what could make this moment worth getting through
Relaxation: a body-based step I can take
One thing in the moment: what I will focus on fully
A short vacation: a brief break I can take and when I will return
Encouragement: words I would say to a friend in this spot
Which letters I will try first

title: Turning the Mind Practice
summary: Helps a client notice when they have turned away from acceptance and choose to turn back toward it.
goal: Build the habit of noticing resistance and making a fresh commitment to accept reality.
body_md: Turning the mind is a choice made again and again, not a one-time decision. Ask the client to name where they notice themselves resisting, such as sulking, arguing in their head or refusing to engage, then pair the commitment with a body cue like opening the hands. Check in on it weekly and go easy on slips, since noticing is the skill.

fields.label: Something I keep fighting or refusing to accept
How I can tell I have turned away (thoughts, body, actions)
What I lose when I stay turned away
What turning my mind toward acceptance would look like today
A body cue that can remind me to turn back
When I will practice and who could remind me

title: One-Mindfully Focus Practice
summary: Trains a client to do one thing at a time and gently return attention when it drifts to something else.
goal: Build a practical routine for single-tasking and for noticing and returning without self-criticism.
body_md: One-mindfully is the how skill of doing one thing with full attention. Start with a five-minute task the client chooses and count the returns, not the drifts, since each return is the skill. Many clients with attention difficulties decide they are failing, so reframe drift as the opportunity to practice. Pair with a timer or body-double if useful.

fields.label: The one task I will do for this practice
How long I will do it (start small)
What pulled my attention away
How many times I noticed and came back
What I did to come back
What made it easier or harder today
What I will try tomorrow

title: Friendship Recipe Card
summary: The child writes and decorates a recipe card listing the ingredients of a good friend and a good friendship.
goal: Help a child name what they want and offer in friendships.
body_md: Give the child a blank recipe card and markers. Ingredients might include sharing, listening, and taking turns, with a stir-in step for fixing mistakes. The parent joins by writing a recipe for being a good family member, then they swap cards and read them aloud. Use the card later to talk about a specific friendship the child is thinking about.

fields.label: The name of my friendship recipe is...
Three ingredients a good friend has are...
One ingredient I already bring is...
One ingredient I want to add is...
What do I do when the recipe goes wrong?
Who would I like to share this recipe with?

title: Values Versus Goals Sorter
summary: A sorting sheet that separates ongoing values from finishable goals and links the two.
goal: Help the client see values as directions and goals as steps along them.
body_md: Ask the client to list things they want in their life and then sort each into a goal, something that can be finished, or a value, something to keep living out. Link each goal to a value it serves. This often clears up why a goal feels hollow or why a missed goal feels like a failed life, and gives you a clearer start on committed action.

fields.label: Things I want in my life right now
Which of these can be finished or checked off (goals)
Which of these are ways I want to keep living (values)
A goal and the value it serves
A goal that does not seem to match any value of mine
A value I could act on today without finishing anything

title: Low-Energy Day Menu for Couples
summary: A menu of small, agreed ways to share a day when one partner's energy and interest are low.
goal: Use it to help partners respond to low mood with options both can live with instead of pressure or distance.
body_md: Have the partner with low mood write what feels doable and the other write what they can offer. Avoid framing items as a fix. Smaller items often work better than ambitious ones, and many partners need permission to lower the bar. Check whether the listener feels shut out, and plan for how to revisit the menu.

fields.label: Partner A: on a low-energy day, what feels doable for me.
Partner B: what I can offer on a low-energy day without taking over.
Words that feel kind to me on a hard day, and words that do not.
One small thing we can do together that asks very little.
What I do when my partner's mood is low and I feel helpless.
A sign that tells us it is time to bring in more support.
How we will check in on the menu in a week.

title: Family Meeting Agenda Sheet
summary: A simple agenda parents can use for a brief weekly family meeting with turns, appreciation and one shared plan.
goal: Give the family a predictable, calm space to plan and solve problems together.
body_md: Suggest keeping meetings under twenty minutes and ending on something enjoyable. Coach the parent to listen first, let each person speak without interruption, and pick one small change at a time. Review how the first meeting went, since the format often needs adjusting.

fields.label: Something each person appreciated this week
What went smoothly at home
One thing we want to change
Ideas from every family member
The one idea we will try this week
Who does what, and when we will check back

title: Avoidance Ledger
summary: A running ledger of what the client avoided, what it cost, and what it protected them from.
goal: Make the price of avoidance visible so the client can choose small steps back.
body_md: Ask the client to jot entries as they happen, even brief ones. Review for patterns and for avoidance that is hard to spot, like leaving early or staying busy. Do not push to stop everything at once; pick one entry to approach in a small way.

fields.label: Something I avoided or put off today
What I was worried would happen
What it cost me in time, mood or plans
What I gained in the short term
A smaller version I could try next time
What I noticed after trying it

title: Problem-Solving Steps Sheet
summary: A six-step sheet that moves a client from naming a problem to trying one option and reviewing how it went.
goal: Use it to turn a stuck, overwhelming problem into one concrete step the client can try.
body_md: Choose a problem that can actually be acted on, not a what-if. Encourage the client to list options without judging them first, since early filtering is where people stall. Help them pick one small step with a day and time. Next session, review what happened and adjust, rather than treating a partial result as failure.

fields.label: The problem, in one or two plain sentences.
What I would like to be different.
Every option I can think of, even the unlikely ones.
The pros and cons of my top two options.
The one step I will try, and when.
What happened, and what I would change.

title: Evening Reflection Log
summary: A short nightly log of what went as planned, what did not, and what to carry into tomorrow.
goal: Give the client a steady daily habit of noticing the day.
duration: Five minutes daily for one week
body_md: Keep it small enough to finish in five minutes, since long logs tend to be dropped by day three. Review the week together and look for patterns in what helped, rather than grading the days. Let the client choose the time of evening that suits them.

fields.label: One thing that went the way I hoped today
One thing that was harder than expected
What I did that I am glad about
What I want to carry into tomorrow
What I can let go of tonight

title: Urgent and Important Sorting Sheet
summary: Sorts a crowded list of demands into four boxes so the client can see what truly needs attention first.
goal: Reduce overwhelm by separating what is urgent from what only feels urgent.
body_md: Have the client brain-dump everything on their mind first, then sort together. Notice which items feel urgent mainly because of worry or pressure from others. Finish by choosing just one or two items for the next day, and name what can wait.

fields.label: Everything on my mind right now
Urgent and important, to do first
Important but not urgent, to schedule
Urgent but not important, to hand off or shorten
Neither, to drop or postpone
The one step I will take tomorrow

title: Transition Ritual Planner
summary: Plans a small repeatable ritual for the moments when the client shifts between work, home and rest.
goal: Help the client mark the edges of the day so stress does not spill over.
body_md: Ask where the day's hardest handoffs happen, such as leaving work or arriving home. Keep each ritual short and concrete, like a walk around the block or changing clothes. Check in next session on which ones were actually used and why the others slipped.

fields.label: The transitions in my day that feel roughest
What I tend to carry from one part of the day into the next
A small ritual that could mark the change
How long it would take and what I need for it
What might get in the way
When I will try it first this week

title: Weekly Review and Reset Sheet
summary: A once-a-week look back at what worked and a short plan for the week ahead.
goal: Build a regular rhythm of reviewing and adjusting rather than starting over.
body_md: Suggest the client complete it at the same time each week, ideally before a session so it can seed the agenda. Encourage curiosity over self-judgment. If a week was rough, focus on the smallest adjustment that would help the next one.

fields.label: What went well this week
What drained me this week
A moment I handled better than I would have before
What I want to do differently next week
The three things that matter most next week
Who or what could support me with them

title: Ask-for-Help Planner
summary: Helps the client decide what to ask for, who to ask and how to word the request.
goal: Make asking for support specific and doable instead of vague and avoided.
body_md: Many clients hold back because they fear being a burden. Explore that belief gently, then keep the request small and clear. Rehearse the wording aloud in session if the client is willing, and plan what to do if the answer is no.

fields.label: Something I could use help with right now
Why I have been hesitant to ask
Who might be a good person to ask
The request in one or two clear sentences
What I will do if they cannot help
How I will thank them or follow up

title: Orienting to Today Card
summary: A pocket card of present-moment facts the client can read when the past feels close.
goal: Give the client a quick way to anchor in today's date, place and safety.
body_md: Build the card in session so the client leaves with it in hand. Keep every prompt in the here and now and do not ask for any details of past events. Practice reading it aloud together, and adjust the wording until it feels believable to the client.

fields.label: Today's date, day and year
Where I am right now
Three things I can see around me
Two people or things that are safe and present today
One thing I can do with my hands to feel steady
A sentence to tell myself: it is today, and I am here

title: Morning Anchor Plan
summary: Plans a short, low-effort morning routine built around one or two anchors the client can reliably do.
goal: Create a gentle start to the day when motivation and energy are low.
body_md: Keep the anchors tiny, such as opening the curtains or a glass of water, so success is likely. Ask the client to choose actions that feel kind, not demanding. If a day is missed, treat it as information about what to shrink, not as a failure.

fields.label: How my mornings usually go
One small thing I could do within ten minutes of waking
Something that makes the morning feel a bit kinder
What might get in my way
How I will remind myself
How I felt on the days I did it

title: Urge Wave Log
summary: Tracks each urge to use a substance: what set it off, how it rose and fell, and what the client did.
goal: Help the client see that urges rise, peak and pass, and learn what helps.
body_md: Normalize urges as a common part of change. Review entries for triggers and times of day, and highlight any time the client rode out an urge, however briefly. Plan next steps together for the situations that were hardest to get through.

fields.label: When the urge showed up and where I was
What happened just before
How strong it felt at the start, from 1 to 10
What I did while it was there
How strong it was after about twenty minutes
What helped, and what I want to try next time

title: Cool-Down Menu Builder
summary: Builds a personal menu of cool-down options sorted by how much time and privacy each one needs.
goal: Give the client a ready choice of ways to ease anger before acting on it.
body_md: Have the client try a few options in session so the menu comes from what actually works for them. Sort by setting, such as at work, in the car or at home. Revisit the menu after real use and prune whatever has not helped.

fields.label: Signs that tell me I need to cool down
Options that take under a minute
Options that take five to ten minutes
Options that need a private space or a walk
The ones that worked best when I tried them
Where I will keep this menu so I can find it fast

title: Panic Recovery Plan Card
summary: A card for the minutes after a wave of panic passes, covering body care, kind self-talk and the next step.
goal: Help the client recover steadily and return to their day afterward.
body_md: Many clients feel shaken and ashamed after panic and then retreat. Complete the card in session when calm, and keep the steps simple. Review how it went and adjust the wording if parts felt unhelpful or hard to remember.

fields.label: What my body feels like in the minutes after panic
Something kind I can say to myself afterward
A small way to care for my body, such as water or a slow walk
One person I can tell or text if I want company
What I will do next in my day
What I learned from this wave to share with my therapist

title: Help and Boundaries Planner
summary: Lists the practical help a new parent wants and plans how to ask for it and set limits with visitors.
goal: Support the client in getting rest and practical help in the early months.
body_md: Many new parents struggle to say what they need or to turn down visitors. Help the client name tasks others could take on and rehearse short phrases for asking or declining. Revisit the plan as the baby's needs and the client's energy shift.

fields.label: Tasks that feel heaviest right now
Tasks someone else could take over
Who might be able to help with each one
How I want visits to go and for how long
Words I can use to ask for help or set a limit
What I will do for my own rest this week

title: Social Event Plan and Review
summary: A before-and-after sheet for a social event: a small goal, a plan, and a look back at what happened.
goal: Help the client approach social events with a plan and learn from how they went.
duration: 20 minutes before and after an event
body_md: Set a modest goal the client can meet, such as staying thirty minutes or asking one person a question. After the event, compare what happened with what was feared, and note what the client did well. Avoid grading the evening on how it felt.

fields.label: The event and what I am expecting
What worries me most about it
My small goal for the event
One thing I can do if I feel uneasy
What actually happened
What I did well and what I will try next time

title: Memory Box Planning Sheet
summary: Plans a keepsake box or small collection that holds meaningful reminders of someone who died.
goal: Give the client a gentle, tangible way to honor a person they lost.
body_md: Let the client set the pace and decide what goes in, and expect feelings to rise while choosing. Keep it a planning conversation first; the client can gather items at home when ready. It also leaves room for a client who needs to wait before taking this on.

fields.label: Who this box is for
Items I might include, such as photos or objects
A song, scent or place that reminds me of them
Words or a note I might add
Where I will keep the box and when I might open it
Who I could share it with if I choose

title: Pacing and Choice Check-In Sheet
summary: A brief check-in the client can use to notice their own pace, make choices and ask for a pause.
goal: Reinforce the client's sense of control over pacing in sessions and in daily life.
body_md: Use it at the start or end of a session, never to prompt any account of past events. Affirm every choice the client makes, including pausing or skipping. Invite them to name what helps them feel steady and supported, and honor it consistently.

fields.label: How I am feeling in my body right now
What would help me feel safe in this moment
What I would like more of today
What I would like less of or want to skip
A signal I can use to ask for a pause
A person or place that helps me feel supported

title: Coping Toolbox Packing List
summary: A packing list for a personal coping toolbox, with items for the body, mind, senses and people.
goal: Help the client gather a varied set of coping options they can reach quickly.
body_md: Ask for a range of tools, since one kind rarely works everywhere. Include items the client can use in public and at night. Encourage them to build a physical or phone version, and review which tools got used and which could be swapped.

fields.label: Tools for my body, such as movement or breathing
Tools for my mind, such as a phrase or distraction
Tools for my senses, such as music or a scent
People I can reach out to
What I can use when I am out in public
Where I will keep my toolbox so it is within reach

title: Coach and Cheerleader Plan
summary: Lays out what a supportive person can say and do, and avoid, while the client practices facing a fear.
goal: Help the client direct a helper who encourages without taking over.
body_md: Invite the support person to a session if the client agrees, or have the client share this sheet. Be clear about what helps, such as calm encouragement, and what does not, like rescuing or pushing. Review after a practice to refine the roles.

fields.label: The step I am going to practice
Who I would like to support me
What helps most when I am nervous
What is not helpful, even if well meant
A word or signal for slowing down
How we will celebrate after the practice

title: Worry Pros and Cons Sheet
summary: A two-sided sheet that lets a client weigh what they believe worrying does for them against what it costs.
goal: Use it to surface beliefs about worry itself so you can test them together.
body_md: Many clients quietly believe worry protects them or shows they care. Ask for the honest advantages before the costs so they do not feel argued with. Then look for a belief you can turn into an experiment, such as trying a worry-free evening and noticing what happens. Revisit the sheet after the experiment instead of settling the question in one sitting.

fields.label: A worry I have had a lot lately.
What I believe worrying about it does for me.
What worrying about it costs me (time, sleep, mood, relationships).
What I notice when I worry less about it, even briefly.
One belief about worry I could test this week.

title: Rational Role-Play Script
summary: A script format for two voices, one holding the old thought and one answering it, played out loud with the clinician.
goal: Use it to help a client hear a balanced reply to a belief when the head knowledge has not yet felt true.
body_md: Begin with the client playing the rational voice while you voice the old thought, so they practice answering. Then swap, with you modeling a reply and the client pushing back as the old thought as strongly as it feels. Stop if the client becomes flooded and return to the script on paper. Roles should be chosen by the client, who keeps the pace.

fields.label: The old thought, worded as strongly as it feels.
How much I believe it right now, from 0 to 100.
My best reply when I play the balanced voice.
The part of the old thought that still pulls hardest.
What helped most when we swapped roles.
How much I believe the old thought now, from 0 to 100.

title: Then Versus Now Reminder Card
summary: A pocket card where a client records present-day facts, a safe person, and one grounding step to use when a reminder hits.
goal: Use it to support stabilizing when reminders pull a client out of the present.
body_md: Complete the card together in session and keep it about the present only. It does not ask for any detail of what happened, and you should say so up front. Help the client choose facts that are easy to check, such as the date, the room and who is nearby. Rehearse using the card once and revise anything that does not feel steady.

fields.label: Today's date and the place where I am.
Three things I can see right now that tell me I am here.
One person or place that is safe for me today.
A sentence that reminds me this is a memory and not now.
One grounding step I can do in under a minute.
What I want to do for myself after the moment passes.

title: Could Happen, Would Cope Sheet
summary: A sheet that pairs a feared outcome with how likely it seems and, more importantly, how the client would handle it.
goal: Use it to shift a client's focus from only predicting danger to trusting their ability to cope.
body_md: Anxious predictions often stop at the feared moment. Ask the client to continue the story past it, step by step, with the people and skills they could draw on. Notice any need to cover every angle in advance and name it kindly. Return later to compare what they predicted with what happened.

fields.label: The thing I am afraid could happen.
How likely it seems right now, from 0 to 10.
If it did happen, the first thing I would do.
Who or what I could lean on.
A time I coped with something hard that I did not expect.
How likely it seems now, and how well I think I could cope.

title: Task Start Thought Record
summary: A short thought record for the moment before starting a task, capturing the thought that delays starting and a helpful reply.
goal: Use it to catch the in-the-moment thoughts that keep a client from beginning a task.
duration: Five minutes per task for one week
body_md: Keep it short enough to use on a phone note or index card, since long forms get skipped. Look for recurring thoughts such as it will take forever or I will do it better later. Help the client write a reply they believe and a tiny first action, like opening the document for two minutes. Review patterns weekly and adapt the replies.

fields.label: The task I am about to start.
The thought that pops up when I think about starting.
What I feel and where I feel it.
A more useful reply to that thought.
The tiny first action I will take now.
What happened after I started.

title: Permission-Giving Thoughts Record
summary: A thought record for the lines a client tells themselves to allow substance use, with a reply and a different action for each.
goal: Use it to help a client spot and answer the thoughts that make an urge feel like a decision already made.
body_md: Permission-giving thoughts often sound reasonable, such as just this once or I earned it. Help the client name their own wording rather than a generic list. Write replies together that are honest and not preachy, and pair each with an action. Review the record without shame when substance use happened, treating it as information about which thoughts were strongest.

fields.label: The situation and the urge I noticed.
The thought that gave me permission.
What I wanted the substance use to do for me in that moment.
A reply that is honest about what usually follows.
What I could do instead that meets the same need.
How strong the urge was before and after, from 0 to 10.

title: Hostile Interpretation Alternatives Sheet
summary: A sheet for listing several other explanations for another person's behavior before the client reacts.
goal: Use it to widen a client's reading of others' intentions and create a gap before they act.
body_md: Start with a recent moment when the client assumed someone meant to disrespect them. Make it safe to say the first reading was reasonable, then ask for three more possibilities, including dull ones. Look at what each reading predicts about the client's own response. Practice on a past event before using it in the moment.

fields.label: What the other person did or said.
What I assumed they meant.
What I felt, and what I wanted to do.
Three other possible explanations.
What I would do if the most neutral one were true.
How the situation might go if I choose that response.

title: Avoided Places Return Plan
summary: A plan that lists places a client avoids after panic, ranks them, and schedules a first return with a prediction to test.
goal: Use it to help a client rebuild a normal range of places, one at a time and at a pace they choose.
body_md: Ask the client to list every place they avoid or enter only with conditions, then rank them together. Choose a first step they rate as challenging but doable, and write down the prediction. Plan how long to stay so the visit is not cut short by the first wave of fear. Review what was learned each week and let the client set the next step.

fields.label: Places I avoid or only go to with conditions.
My ranking, from easiest to hardest.
The first place I will return to, and when.
What I predict will happen there.
How long I plan to stay.
What actually happened, and what that tells me.

title: Good Enough Parent Thought Record
summary: A thought record for the moments a parent decides they are failing, with a prompt to restate the standard they are using.
goal: Use it to help a parent notice unrealistic standards and set fairer ones for themselves.
body_md: Parents often hold a standard they would never set for another parent. Help the client catch the all-or-nothing wording, such as always or never, in the thought. Ask what a good enough day would look like and what a trusted friend would say. Keep the tone warm, and treat any wish to repair with the child as a strength to build on.

fields.label: The moment I thought I was failing as a parent.
The exact thought and how much I believed it, from 0 to 100.
The standard I was holding myself to.
What a fair, good enough standard would look like.
What I did well in that situation, even if small.
A reply I can use next time.

title: Achievement Discounting Sheet
summary: A sheet for noticing how a client waves away their own successes and writing what the success says when taken at face value.
goal: Use it to counter the habit of dismissing good outcomes as luck, easy or not counting.
body_md: Clients with low self-regard often keep a double ledger where mistakes count fully and successes do not. Ask for one recent success and what they said to downplay it. Then have them write the same event as if it had happened to someone else. Revisit the sheet weekly so it becomes a habit rather than a single task.

fields.label: Something that went well recently, however small.
What I said to wave it away.
What I would say about this if a friend had done it.
What it shows about my skills or effort.
How much of me believes that, from 0 to 100.
One more thing this week I will let count.

title: Small Talk Experiment Ladder
summary: A ladder of brief conversation experiments, each with a prediction, a try, and a note on what really happened.
goal: Use it to give a client low-stakes ways to test feared reactions in everyday exchanges.
body_md: Build the ladder from the client's real days, such as greeting a neighbor or asking a cashier a question. Write down what they expect the other person to do, and what they will treat as the sign of success. Keep the early rungs very small. Afterward, compare what happened with the prediction and avoid grading how smooth the client sounded.

fields.label: Brief conversations that feel doable, from easiest to hardest.
The one I will try first, and when.
What I predict the other person will do or think.
What I will do, and what I will not do to feel safer.
What actually happened.
What this tells me about my prediction.

title: Grief Should Statements Sheet
summary: A sheet for naming the rules a client holds about how they ought to grieve and reworking each into a kinder preference.
goal: Use it to ease pressure from rigid expectations about the pace and shape of grief.
body_md: Grief carries many unspoken rules, such as I should be over this by now. Invite the client to say theirs without judgment, and honor that culture and family shape these expectations. Work on softening the rule rather than denying the loss. Notice if the rules point to guilt and offer to return to it in a separate session.

fields.label: A should I tell myself about how I ought to grieve.
Where I learned this rule.
How it makes me feel when I do not meet it.
How I would respond if someone I love held this rule.
A kinder way to word it that leaves room for me.
One thing I will let myself do this week.

title: Support Network Prediction Check
summary: A pacing sheet for choosing one supportive person, predicting how reaching out might go, and picking a small, chosen step.
goal: Use it to help a client test whether support is available, at a pace they set and with no details required.
body_md: This tool is about present-day support and does not ask the client to describe or write out what happened. Let the client set the pace and the level of sharing, which can be as small as a text saying they want company. Talk through what they would want from the person. Remind them they can stop or change the plan at any time and review it together.

fields.label: One person I might feel safe reaching out to.
What I would want from them (company, a call, practical help).
What I predict might happen if I reached out.
The smallest step I could take, if I choose to.
Something I could say that shares only what I want to share.
What I would do for myself if it does not go as hoped.

title: Coping Skill Match Chart
summary: A chart that matches each coping skill a client already uses to the kinds of situations where it works best.
goal: Use it to help a client choose the right skill for the moment instead of defaulting to one.
body_md: Start with what the client already does, including habits they judge as poor, and note what each one does for them. Then sort by situation, such as feeling stuck, flooded or lonely, and see where gaps remain. Add one or two new skills to try, and keep the chart short enough to use in real life. Review it after a week of trials.

fields.label: Skills I already use when I feel stressed.
What each one does for me (calms, distracts, energizes, connects).
Situations where my usual skills do not work well.
A skill I would like to try for those moments.
When I will try it this week.
How it went, and where it fits on my chart.

title: Appearance Avoidance Return Plan
summary: A plan listing activities a client skips because of appearance worries, ranked and scheduled one step at a time.
goal: Use it to help a client rejoin activities they value that appearance worries have crowded out.
body_md: Begin with what the client misses, such as swimming, photos or a night out, and why it matters to them. Rank activities by difficulty and choose one step. Record the prediction and the safety habits they are likely to use, then decide which to drop for the experiment. Review how it felt to be present, not how they looked, and keep the pace theirs.

fields.label: Activities I skip or cut short because of how I think I look.
Why each one matters to me.
My ranking, from easiest to hardest.
The first one I will return to, and when.
What I predict will happen, and what I do to feel safer.
What happened, and what it was like to be there.

title: Five Senses Present Moment Pause
summary: A brief contact-with-the-present-moment practice that moves attention through the senses, one at a time.
goal: Give the client a portable way to come back to what is here right now.
body_md: Walk the client through noticing a few things they can see, hear, feel, smell and taste, slowly and without judging them. Practice it together in session first so it is familiar before it is needed elsewhere. If attention drifts, the noticing of drifting is the practice, so reassure the client that wandering is expected and not a failure.

fields.label: Things I can see right now
Things I can hear
Things I can feel through my skin or my body
Any smell or taste I can notice
How my attention moved while I did this
A time this week I could use this pause

title: Obstacle Plan for Committed Action
summary: A planning sheet that names the thoughts and feelings likely to show up and how to take the step anyway.
goal: Prepare the client to act on a values-based step when discomfort appears.
body_md: Start with one small, specific step tied to a value, then ask the client what thoughts, feelings and practical barriers might show up. For each, plan a willing response, such as noticing the thought or making room for the feeling. Keep the step small enough to be realistic, and review what happened next session without treating a missed step as failure, just information about workability.

fields.label: The value I want to act on
One small, specific step I will take and when
Thoughts that might show up and try to stop me
Feelings that might show up
Practical obstacles that could get in the way
What I will do with each one so I can still take the step
How I will check in on how it went

title: Safe Anchors Pacing Practice
summary: A stabilizing sheet that pairs present-moment anchors with a pace the client chooses.
goal: Build steady footing in the present and respect the client's pace.
body_md: This stays in the present: the client names things in the room that tell them they are here and now, such as the feel of the chair or a color they can see, and sets a pace for the practice. Nothing here asks about what happened. If the client drifts or feels flooded, pause and return to the anchors together, and let them decide when to stop.

fields.label: Something in this room that tells me I am here and now
A way my feet or body feel supported right now
A pace that feels okay for me today (slow, medium, short)
A signal I can give if I want to pause
A person or place that helps me feel steadier
What I notice in my body after naming these anchors
If I feel unsafe, I can call or text 988 or tell someone I trust

title: Anxiety as Background Music Practice
summary: A metaphor sheet that treats anxious noise as background music while the client keeps doing what matters.
goal: Practice doing a valued activity with anxious sensations present.
body_md: Offer the image of anxiety as music playing in the next room: it can be loud, and the client can still cook, talk or work. Ask the client to rate the volume and then name what they did anyway. The goal is not turning it down. Check that the client does not hear this as being told to ignore anxiety, and keep inviting willingness rather than suppression.

fields.label: What the background music of my anxiety sounds like today
How loud it was, from soft to very loud
A valued activity I did or could do with the music on
What my mind said while I did it
What it was like to let the music play
One more thing I could do while it plays

title: Willing Start for Tasks Practice
summary: A practice for starting a task with boredom or restlessness present, tied to a value behind the task.
goal: Help the client begin a valued task without waiting to feel ready.
body_md: Pick one task the client keeps putting off and link it to a value behind it. Have them name the thoughts and restless feelings that show up at the start, then commit to two minutes of starting with those present. Keep the first step very small and check in on how starting felt, not how much got done, so effort is recognized.

fields.label: A task I keep putting off
The value that sits behind this task
Thoughts and feelings that show up when I think about starting
My two-minute starting step
What I noticed in the first two minutes
What I would like to keep going or do next

title: Urge Notice and Name Log
summary: A log for noticing a substance use urge, naming its parts and choosing the next move by values.
goal: Help the client pause with an urge and choose a response that fits their values.
duration: Five minutes daily for several weeks
body_md: The client records each urge as it happens: what was going on, what the urge felt like in the body, the thoughts attached, and what they chose to do. The log gives you something to look at together rather than a verdict on their week. Review it without judgment, and stay curious about urges that were followed as well as those that were not.

fields.label: Where I was and what was happening when the urge showed up
What the urge felt like in my body
Thoughts that came along with it
How long I noticed it before I did anything
What I chose to do next
What I care about that this choice served or cost me

title: Doubt Visiting Response Pause
summary: A pause sheet for noticing doubt, welcoming it without a ritual and choosing a values-based action.
goal: Help the client practice making room for doubt without acting on it.
body_md: Frame doubt as a visitor who can stay while the client gets on with the day. Have them name the doubt, notice the pull to check, seek reassurance or do a ritual, and pick one small valued action instead. Go at the client's pace, start with low-intensity doubts, and keep this as practice you do together rather than a rule the client must obey.

fields.label: The doubt that showed up
What my mind said I needed to do about it
The urge I noticed in my body
What I did instead, or what I could do instead
What I care about that I moved toward
How it felt to let the doubt stay

title: Panic Aftermath Kindness Debrief
summary: A short debrief sheet for the hours after a panic surge that focuses on self-kindness and returning to life.
goal: Help the client respond to themselves kindly and get back to what matters.
body_md: Use this in the hours after a panic surge to move the client away from replaying it and toward steadier footing. They note what they felt, what they told themselves, and what a caring friend would say. Review it together to find the next small valued step, and keep the tone warm so they do not read the debrief as a test.

fields.label: What I noticed in my body during the surge
What my mind said about it afterward
What a caring friend would say to me
One kind thing I can do for myself right now
What I was doing before this that matters to me
A small step I can take to get back to it

title: Defusing Parent Verdicts Practice
summary: A defusion sheet for harsh verdicts a parent hears from their mind, paired with the parent they want to be.
goal: Help the parent hold judgments loosely and act on their parenting values.
body_md: Many parents carry a loud inner commentary after a hard moment. Ask them to write the verdict, add the phrase I am having the thought that, and name one value they want to parent from. Then plan one small act that fits that value. Keep it about the parent's own mind and choices, not their child's behavior.

fields.label: A verdict my mind gave me about my parenting
The same verdict, starting with I am having the thought that
How the thought feels when I say it this way
A value I want to parent from
One small thing I could do this week that fits that value
What I might say to myself when the verdict shows up again

title: Critic's Greatest Hits Defusion Sheet
summary: A defusion sheet that lists the inner critic's repeating lines like a playlist and tries each one at a distance.
goal: Help the client see the critic's lines as familiar and workable to carry.
body_md: Ask the client to list the lines their inner critic repeats, as if it were a playlist of greatest hits, and notice which ones seem to play most. Then try a few defusion moves, like thanking the mind or singing the line, and see what is workable. Stay alert to a client who becomes more self-critical for not doing it well, and slow down if so.

fields.label: The top three lines my inner critic plays
When each one tends to play
How I usually respond when it plays
A defusion move I tried on one line
What happened when I tried it
What I would like to do when the critic plays next time

title: Bringing Anxiety Along Social Plan
summary: A planning sheet for going to a social event with anxiety coming along, guided by what the client values.
goal: Help the client move toward people with anxiety present rather than waiting for it to leave.
body_md: Have the client choose a social situation that matters to them, then plan for anxiety to come along instead of trying to remove it. They name the value, the thoughts and sensations to expect, and one small action. Choose a step small enough to try, and afterward focus on what they did and cared about, not how anxious they felt.

fields.label: A social situation that matters to me
The value I want to show up with
Thoughts and feelings I expect to bring along
One small action I will take there
What I will do if anxiety gets loud
What I noticed afterward about what I did

title: Hooked in Conflict Pause Practice
summary: A pause sheet for noticing the moment of getting hooked in a conflict and choosing a response from values.
goal: Help the client notice hooks in conflict and choose how they respond.
body_md: Ask the client to look back at a recent conflict and find the moment they got hooked, such as a thought, a feeling or an urge to react. Then explore a pause there and what they would want to do from their values. Keep the focus on the client's own responses and choices, and avoid turning it into a ruling on the other person.

fields.label: A recent conflict I want to look at
The moment I felt hooked
The thought, feeling or urge that showed up
What I did in response
What I want my response to stand for in this relationship
What I could do at the hook point next time

title: Safe Place and Support Anchors Practice
summary: A stabilizing practice that gathers present-moment anchors, safe places and people the client can lean on.
goal: Build a client-chosen set of safety and support anchors at the client's pace.
body_md: This tool stays with safety, support and pacing, and never asks about what happened. The client names a place that feels safe, a person or two who help, and a simple anchor in the present. Complete the last prompt about 988 in session, so you can talk it through together. If the client has a history of child abuse, check your reporting duties around any new disclosure.

fields.label: A place, real or imagined, where I feel safer
A person or two I can lean on
Something in the room that reminds me I am here now
A pace for this work that feels right for me
What I notice in my body when I picture my safe place
If I feel unsafe or in crisis, I can call or text 988

title: Notice, Make Room, Move Practice
summary: A three-step practice for hard moments: notice what is here, make room for it, and move toward what matters.
goal: Give the client a simple routine for hard moments that ends in a valued action.
body_md: Walk the client through three steps: notice thoughts and feelings that are present, make room for them with a breath or a kind word, and then move toward a small action that fits a value. Practice with a mildly hard moment first. Make sure the client does not use the room-making step as another way to push feelings away.

fields.label: A hard moment I want to practice with
What I notice in my thoughts and body
How I can make room for these without fighting them
A value I want to move toward in this moment
One small action I can take next
How I will remind myself of these three steps

title: Values Beyond the Mirror Plan
summary: A plan that moves attention from appearance thoughts toward what the client wants their days to stand for.
goal: Help the client hold appearance thoughts loosely while acting on their values.
body_md: Ask the client to notice thoughts about appearance as passing mental events, then turn to what they want their day to be about, such as connection, creativity or play. Pair one value with one small action. Keep the conversation off judging or changing the body, and focus instead on what the client wants to do with their time and energy.

fields.label: An appearance thought that shows up often
How I can name it, such as I am having the thought that
What I want my days to stand for
One thing I did or could do this week that fits that value
What I noticed when I put my attention there
Who or what could support me in doing more of it

title: Problem Solving Steps Sheet
summary: Breaks one stuck problem into describing it, checking the facts, setting a goal, brainstorming and trying a solution.
goal: Move a client from rumination about a problem to one concrete step they can try.
body_md: Use this when the client is stuck in the problem rather than the solution. Have them describe the problem in plain observable terms first, since vague problems produce vague plans. Encourage a long brainstorm list before any judging, then pick one option and make it small enough to try this week. Review what happened and adjust together.

fields.label: The problem, described in plain facts
What I want to be different (my goal)
Facts I may be missing or assuming
Every possible solution, including silly ones
The option I will try and why
The first small step and when I will take it
How I will tell whether it helped
If it did not work, what I will change

title: Emotion Wave Mindfulness Log
summary: Tracks a feeling as it rises, peaks and falls while the client observes it without acting on it.
goal: Show the client that emotions move like waves and can be observed rather than obeyed.
body_md: Mindfulness of current emotions asks the client to step back and watch a feeling as an observer. Have them fill this in during or right after an emotion, and compare entries over time to see how often a feeling rose and fell without action. Clients may judge the feeling, so remind them to describe it rather than grade it.

fields.label: The emotion I noticed and what set it off
Where I felt it in my body
The urge that came with it
What I did instead of acting on the urge
How strong it was at the start (0 to 10)
How strong it was at the peak (0 to 10)
How strong it was when it eased (0 to 10)
What I noticed about how it moved

title: Pushing Away Mental Box
summary: Sets up a mental box for putting a painful topic aside for now, with a plan for returning to it later.
goal: Give the client a short-term way to set a topic down so they can function, without avoiding it for good.
body_md: Pushing away is a short-term distress tolerance skill, and the plan to come back is what keeps it from becoming avoidance. Have the client picture the box in detail, decide what goes in, and set a time and a person for returning to it. Review in session whether the box is being used to get through a work block or to dodge for weeks.

fields.label: The topic I want to set aside for now
What my mental box looks like (size, material, lid)
How I will put the topic in and close it
What I will do to stay busy while it is set aside
When and where I will take it back out
Who I can talk it through with when I do
Signs I am using the box too long

title: Pacing and Support Wise Mind Plan
summary: Uses wise mind to pace a week so a client with trauma history keeps steady footing and leans on supports.
goal: Help the client choose a manageable pace and name the people and skills that keep them steady.
body_md: Keep this firmly on the stabilizing side: it asks about pace, supports and skills, never about what happened. Use wise mind to decide what the client can take on this week and what to postpone. Prompts about safety should be completed in session so you can talk through the 988 line together, and remind the client they can pause at any point.

fields.label: What a manageable week looks like for me right now
What my emotional mind wants to push me to do too fast
What my reasonable mind says I should do
What my wise mind says about pace this week
Things I will postpone or do in smaller pieces
People I can reach out to for support
A skill I can use if I feel overwhelmed
If I feel unsafe or in danger of hurting myself, I can call or text 988 and I will tell my therapist

title: Long-Term Positives Values Ladder
summary: Links a client's values to small steps that build positives over weeks, using the accumulate long-term skill.
goal: Reconnect a client with low mood to what matters to them through steps small enough to start.
body_md: Accumulating positives in the long term starts with values, then goals, then one small action. Ask the client to name what matters even if it feels flat today, and let them choose a step that feels almost too small. Clients often hold back on the first rung, so celebrate any attempt. Prompts about hopelessness should be completed in session.
